**Pie charts:** a sector’s share in degrees ÷ 360 gives its fraction; 72° = 20%, 54° = 15%, 36° = 10%. **Line and bar charts:** read values carefully from the scale and note whether the axis starts at zero. **Radar charts** plot several categories around a centre; treat each spoke as a column of a table.
Mistakes seen in Mains.
points: Taking percentage of the wrong base (previous year vs current year).
Adding percentages of different bases.
Treating "2 more" and "2% more" alike.
Not counting overlap in caselets.

notes.p: DI checklist.
points: Convert caselet text into a table first.
Fill missing cells before answering.
Know fraction-percent equivalents to 1/12.
Percent change = change ÷ old × 100.
DS: unique answer needed; do not fully solve.
Approximate when options are far apart.

chapters.title: Number series: all patterns & new pattern

cards.title: Pattern families
cards.body: Check in this order: **differences** (and differences of differences), **multiplication/division**, **×a ± b mixes**, **squares/cubes ± n**, **primes**, **alternate (two interleaved) series**.

cards.title: Common patterns
points: n² ± k, n³ ± k, n(n + 1)
×0.5, ×1, ×1.5, ×2 … (decimal multipliers)
Differences forming squares, cubes, primes or AP/GP
Alternate terms forming two series

cards.title: New pattern question
cards.body:
Series I: 4, 6, 15, 52.5 (×1.5, ×2.5, ×3.5).
Series II starts at 8 with the same rule: 8, 12, 30, 105. Third term = **30**.

cards.title: Growth rate tells the family
cards.body: Slow growth → differences. Roughly doubling → ×2 ± k. Explosive growth → increasing multipliers. Up-and-down → alternate series.

cards.q: Find the wrong number: 4, 9, 25, 49, 120, 169
cards.explain: Squares of primes 2, 3, 5, 7, 11, 13; 11² = 121.

notes.p:
Number series give 5 questions in most bank Prelims and appear in Mains. The patterns are finite; what costs time is trying them in a random order. Use a fixed checklist, and look at how fast the series grows before calculating anything.

A good habit: spend at most 10 seconds testing differences; if nothing appears, switch to ratios. If neither works in 30 seconds, mark the question and move on.

Write the first differences under the series. If they are not constant, take differences again.

**Worked example 1:** 7, 10, 16, 25, 37, ?
Differences 3, 6, 9, 12 → next 15 → **52**.

**Worked example 2:** 6, 7, 11, 20, 36, ?
Differences 1, 4, 9, 16 (squares) → next 25 → **61**.

Differences may also be primes (2, 3, 5, 7…), cubes, or a geometric series.

When terms roughly double or triple, test ×n ± k.

**Worked example 3:** 2, 5, 11, 23, 47, ? → ×2 + 1 → **95**.

**Worked example 4:** 1, 2, 6, 24, 120, ? → ×2, ×3, ×4, ×5 → ×6 → **720**.

Decimal multipliers (×0.5, ×1.5, ×2.5) are popular in Mains; a series that rises slowly and then sharply often uses them.

**Worked example 5:** 2, 5, 4, 10, 8, 20, ?
Odd positions: 2, 4, 8 (×2); even positions: 5, 10, 20 (×2). Next odd term = **16**.

Squares/cubes ± a constant: 10, 26, 50, 82, ? = 3² + 1, 5² + 1, 7² + 1, 9² + 1 → 11² + 1 = **122**.

In **new pattern** questions, find the rule from Series I, apply it to a new starting value, and report the asked term. Compute only up to that term.

In **wrong number** questions, find the rule from the majority of terms. Fix the rule using the first few terms, then predict each term; the one that does not match is wrong (usually off by 1–2).
points: Never assume the first term is wrong; check the middle ones first.

notes.h: Worked drill: identifying the rule fast
notes.p:
**Worked example 6:** 120, 60, 20, 5, 1, ?
Ratios: ÷2, ÷3, ÷4, ÷5 → next ÷6 → **1/6**. A falling series with shrinking ratios signals increasing divisors.

**Worked example 7:** 3, 8, 15, 24, 35, ?
These are n² − 1 for n = 2 to 6 → 7² − 1 = **48** (also: differences 5, 7, 9, 11, 13).

**Worked example 8:** 11, 13, 17, 19, 23, ? → consecutive primes → **29**.

When two rules seem to fit, prefer the one that explains every term, and check it against the options.
Series checklist.
points: Look at the growth rate first.
Differences → second differences.
×n ± k and increasing multipliers.
Squares, cubes, primes ± constant.
Up-and-down → alternate series.
New pattern: copy the rule, compute only the needed term.

cards.title: The heaviest-weight topic
cards.body: Puzzles and seating carry **15–25 marks** in prelims and more in mains. Types: linear row (one or two rows), circular/square/rectangular table, floor/flat, box/stack, scheduling (days/months) and comparison puzzles.

cards.title: Direction in a circle
cards.body: Facing the **centre**: left = clockwise, right = anticlockwise. Facing **outside**: it reverses. In a row facing north, the person's right is your right; facing south, it is your left.

cards.title: Start with fixed clues
cards.body: Begin with the clue that fixes a position ("A sits at an extreme end", "B lives on floor 3"). Then use clues linked to already-placed people. Leave negative clues ("C does not sit next to D") for the end to eliminate cases.

cards.title: Make cases, not guesses
cards.body: When a clue allows two positions, draw **Case 1 and Case 2** side by side and continue both. Usually one case breaks within two or three clues. This is faster than restarting.

cards.title: Row counting
points: Total = left rank + right rank − 1
Persons between A and B = |rank difference| − 1
In a circle of n, opposite = n/2 places away

cards.q: In a row facing north, P is 3rd from the left and 8th from the right. How many people are in the row?
Eight people sit around a circle facing the centre. Moving to someone's immediate left means moving:
cards.explain: When facing the centre, a person's left is in the clockwise direction.

cards.q: A 5-floor building (floor 1 at bottom): A lives on floor 3; B two floors above A; C immediately below B; D on an odd floor other than A's; E on the remaining floor. Who lives on floor 2?
cards.explain: A = 3, B = 5, C = 4, D must be on floor 1 (the only free odd floor), so E is on floor 2.

notes.h: Why puzzles matter and the main types
notes.p: Puzzles and seating arrangements make up the **largest share of Reasoning** in both Prelims and Mains, often 15–25 questions. Each puzzle carries 5 questions, so solving one correctly is worth 5 marks, while abandoning it halfway is worth zero. That is why a reliable method matters more than speed.
points: **Linear seating:** one or two rows, facing north or south.
**Circular/square/rectangular seating:** facing the centre, outside, or mixed.
**Floor and flat puzzles:** who lives on which floor.
**Scheduling:** months, days, years.
**Box/stack puzzles, comparison puzzles, multi-variable puzzles** (person + city + colour).

notes.h: A step-by-step method that works for every puzzle
notes.p: Follow the same steps every time so you do not miss clues under pressure.
points: Step 1: read all clues once and **draw the frame** (positions 1–7, floors 1–5, a circle).
Step 2: start with **definite clues** ("A sits at an extreme end", "B lives on floor 3").
Step 3: link clues that share a person and build **cases** when a clue allows two places.
Step 4: test each case against the remaining clues; strike out the case that breaks a clue.
Step 5: place leftover people using **negative clues** ("U is not a neighbour of T").
Step 6: re-read every clue against the final diagram before answering.

notes.p:
In a **row facing north**, your left is the viewer's left. In a row facing south, left and right are reversed.

In a **circle facing the centre**, a person's **right is anticlockwise** and **left is clockwise**. Facing outside, it is the opposite. 'Second to the right' means skip one person and take the next in that direction.

Seven people P, Q, R, S, T, U, V sit in a row facing **north** (positions 1–7 from left).
1. S sits at an extreme end.
2. Exactly two people sit between S and T.
3. R sits immediately to the right of T.
4. Q sits third to the left of V.
5. U sits somewhere to the right of R.

**Case A (S at 1):** clue 2 → T at 4; clue 3 → R at 5. Clue 4: possible (Q, V) pairs are (2, 5), (3, 6), (4, 7); 5 is R and 4 is T, so **Q = 3, V = 6**. Left: positions 2 and 7 for P and U. Clue 5: U is right of R (5) → **U = 7**, **P = 2**.
Result: **S P Q T R V U**.

**Case B (S at 7):** clue 2 → T at 4; R at 5; Q = 3, V = 6. Left: positions 1 and 2. Clue 5 needs U to the right of R, but 1 and 2 are left of R → **case rejected**.

Final answer: S P Q T R V U. Who sits in the middle? **T**.

Five people A–E live on floors 1 (bottom) to 5 (top), one per floor.
1. B lives on an odd-numbered floor above D.
2. Only one person lives between B and C.
3. A lives immediately above C.
4. E does not live on floor 1.

Clue 1 → B is on 3 or 5 (not 1, since D must be below).
**Try B = 3:** clue 2 → C = 1 or 5. If C = 1, A = 2, leaving no floor below B for D except 1 and 2, both taken ✗. If C = 5, A would be 6 ✗. So B ≠ 3.
**Try B = 5:** clue 2 → C = 3; clue 3 → A = 4. D and E take floors 1 and 2; clue 4 → **E = 2, D = 1**. D is below B ✓.
Final (top to bottom): **5 B, 4 A, 3 C, 2 E, 1 D**.
These mistakes break otherwise correct diagrams.
points: Confusing left/right for people facing south or facing outward.
Reading 'two people between' as 'second to the left'.
Dropping a case too early without checking every clue.
Spending 15 minutes on one puzzle; if no progress in 4 minutes, move on.

notes.p: Before every puzzle, remember:
points: Draw the frame first; start with definite clues.
Make cases when a clue allows two positions; eliminate with later clues.
Facing centre: right = anticlockwise, left = clockwise.
Facing south: left and right reverse.
Use negative clues at the end.
Verify every clue against the final arrangement.

cards.title: Draw Venn diagrams
cards.body: Draw the **minimum** overlap the statements force. A conclusion follows only if it is true in **every** possible diagram. A 'possibility' conclusion follows if it is true in **at least one** valid diagram.

cards.title: Definite combinations
points: All + All = All
All + No = No
Some + All = Some
Some + No = Some … not (order reversed)
All A are B → Some A are B and Some B are A

cards.title: Either–or pair
cards.body: If neither conclusion follows on its own, but the two together cover all cases (e.g. 'Some A are B' and 'No A is B'), then **either I or II** follows. Both must be about the same two terms and be complementary.

cards.title: Common traps
cards.body: 'All A are B' does **not** mean 'All B are A'. Two 'Some' statements never give a definite conclusion. A 'No' statement makes the reverse 'possibility' false.

cards.title: Worked example
cards.body:
All pens are books. Some books are bags.
Pens may or may not touch bags, so 'Some pens are bags' does **not** follow. 'Some bags are books' is just the reverse of statement 2, so it **follows**.

cards.q:
All pens are books. Some books are bags.
I. Some pens are bags.  II. Some bags are books.
cards.explain: II is the conversion of 'Some books are bags'. I is only a possibility, not certain.

cards.q:
All cats are dogs. No dog is a rat.
I. No cat is a rat.  II. Some rats being cats is a possibility.
cards.explain: All + No = No, so 'No cat is a rat' is definite, which makes II impossible.

cards.q:
Some A are B. No B is C.
I. Some A are not C.  II. All C being A is a possibility.
cards.explain: Some + No = Some not, so I follows. C is only separated from B, so C can lie fully inside A; II is possible.

notes.p:
You are given statements (assumed true even if they sound absurd) and must decide which conclusions **definitely follow**. Use **Venn diagrams**: draw the minimum overlap that the statements guarantee, then test each conclusion. A conclusion follows only if it is true in **every** possible diagram.

Modern papers also ask **possibility** conclusions ("All A being B is a possibility"). A possibility follows if it is true in **at least one** valid diagram that does not break a statement.
points: **All A are B:** circle A inside B.
**Some A are B:** circles overlap.
**No A is B:** circles are separate.
**Some A are not B:** part of A is outside B.

notes.p: These rules let you answer many questions without drawing.
points: All + All → All (All A are B, All B are C → All A are C).
All + No → No (All A are B, No B is C → No A is C).
Some + All → Some (Some A are B, All B are C → Some A are C).
Some + No → Some not (Some A are B, No B is C → Some A are not C).
Some + Some, or No + No → no definite conclusion.
'All A are B' also gives 'Some A are B' and 'Some B are A'.

notes.p:
**Example 1:** All pens are books. Some books are tables.
Conclusions: I. Some pens are tables. II. Some tables being pens is a possibility.
Diagram: pens inside books; tables overlap books. Tables may or may not touch the pen circle.
I is not certain → **does not follow**. II can be drawn without breaking any statement → **follows**.

**Example 2:** Some cats are dogs. No dog is a rat.
Conclusions: I. Some cats are not rats. II. All rats being cats is a possibility.
The cats that are dogs cannot be rats, so I **follows**. Rats must stay outside dogs, but the cat circle extends outside dogs, so rats can sit inside that part → II **follows**.

**Example 3:** All roses are flowers. No flower is a leaf.
I. No rose is a leaf → All + No = No → **follows**.
II. Some leaves are roses → contradicts I → **does not follow**.

When neither conclusion is definite, check for an **either–or pair**. It applies when both conclusions have the **same two terms** and together cover all possibilities, typically **Some + No** or **Some + Some not**.

**Example 4:** Some boys are girls. Some girls are women.
I. Some boys are women. II. No boy is a woman.
Neither is definite, but one of them must be true (either boys and women overlap or they don't). Answer: **either I or II follows**.

Do not apply either–or if one conclusion already follows definitely.

notes.h: 'Only a few' and other special words
notes.p: **Only a few A are B** means some A are B **and** some A are not B; therefore 'All A are B' is **not even possible**. 'At least some' = some. 'Some A are not B' does not tell you anything about B's relation to A in reverse.
points: 'All A are B' → 'All B are A' is only a possibility, never certain.
'Some A are not B' cannot be reversed to 'Some B are not A'.
A possibility is rejected only if it contradicts a statement.

notes.p: Watch for these.
points: Using real-world knowledge instead of the given statements.
Reversing 'All A are B' into 'All B are A'.
Marking a possibility as false just because it is not certain.
Applying either–or when one conclusion already follows.
Forgetting the 'only a few' restriction.

notes.p: Key rules to remember.
points: Draw the minimum diagram; definite = true in all diagrams.
Possibility = true in at least one valid diagram.
All+All=All; All+No=No; Some+All=Some; Some+No=Some not.
Some+Some and No+No → no definite conclusion.
Either–or: same terms, complementary pair, neither definite.
'Only a few A are B' → 'All A are B' is impossible.

cards.title: Chain rule
cards.body: You can join two terms only through a chain where all signs point the **same way** (>, ≥, = together, or <, ≤, = together). If signs point in opposite directions (A > B < C), there is **no relation** between A and C.

cards.title: Resulting sign
points: > with ≥ or = gives >
≥ with = gives ≥
= with = gives =
Opposite directions: no relation

cards.title: Either–or
cards.body: If conclusions are 'A > B' and 'A = B' and the chain gives A ≥ B, then **either I or II** is true. The same holds for '<' and '=' with ≤.

cards.title: Coded inequality
cards.body: Some questions use symbols like @, #, $ for >, <, =. Decode the symbols once, rewrite the statement in normal signs, and then solve. Do not try to solve in code.

cards.q:
A > B ≥ C = D < E.
I. A > D  II. E > B
cards.explain: A > B ≥ C = D gives A > D. B ≥ C and C < E point in opposite directions, so B and E cannot be compared.

cards.q:
L ≤ M < N; O > N.
I. O > L  II. M < O
cards.explain: L ≤ M < N < O gives O > L and M < O. Both are true.

cards.q:
X ≥ Y.
I. X > Y  II. X = Y
cards.explain: X ≥ Y means X is either greater than or equal to Y: a complementary pair.

notes.p:
Inequality questions give a chain such as P > Q ≥ R = S < T and ask whether conclusions like P > S follow. A conclusion follows only if there is a path between the two elements where **all signs point the same way** (or are '=').

Combine signs along the path: **> with ≥ or = gives >**; **≥ with = gives ≥**; any path containing **opposite directions** (> and <) gives **no relation**.
points: Direct statements: A > B, A < B, A ≥ B, A ≤ B, A = B.
A ≥ B means A > B or A = B.
If no single-direction path exists, the conclusion does not follow.

notes.p:
**Example 1:** P > Q ≥ R = S < T
I. P > S: path P > Q ≥ R = S, all in one direction with a strict '>' → **follows**.
II. T > Q: path Q ≥ R = S < T changes direction at S → **does not follow**.
III. R ≤ Q: given directly as Q ≥ R → **follows**.

**Example 2:** A ≥ B = C, C ≤ D
I. A > C. II. A = C.
Path A ≥ B = C gives **A ≥ C**. Neither I nor II is certain alone, but together they cover A ≥ C → **either I or II follows**.
D vs A: A ≥ C ≤ D has opposite directions → no relation.

Some questions replace signs with symbols. Decode first, then solve normally.

**Example 3:** '@' means '>', '#' means '<', '$' means '=', '%' means '≥', '&' means '≤'.
Statement: M @ N % O $ P → **M > N ≥ O = P**.
Conclusion I: M @ P (M > P). Path M > N ≥ O = P → **true**.
Conclusion II: N & P (N ≤ P). We know N ≥ P, so N ≤ P is not certain → **false**.

Write the decoded chain on rough paper once; do not decode in your head for every conclusion.

Some questions ask which sign must go in a blank so that a conclusion definitely holds.

**Example 4:** J > K __ L ≥ M. Which sign makes 'J > M' definitely true?
The path must keep one direction. Signs **>, ≥ or =** all work (each gives J > M since there is already a strict > at the start). Signs < or ≤ break the direction. Choose the option that matches one of the valid signs and satisfies any second conclusion asked.
These traps are set deliberately.
points: Concluding A > C from A > B < C (opposite directions).
Turning A ≥ B into A > B (it may be equal).
Missing the either–or case when both '>' and '=' are offered.
Decoding symbols wrongly under time pressure.
Ignoring a second statement that links the same elements.

notes.p: The whole chapter in six lines.
points: Same-direction path needed for any conclusion.
> combined with ≥ or = → >.
≥ combined with = → ≥.
Opposite signs → no relation.
A ≥ B with conclusions A > B and A = B → either–or.
Decode symbols once, then solve.

cards.title: Draw a family tree
cards.body: Use a standard notation: **square or + for male, circle or − for female**, horizontal line for siblings, vertical line for generations, double line for married couples. Never solve blood relations in your head.

cards.title: Must-know relations
points: Father's/mother's brother: uncle (paternal/maternal)
Brother's/sister's son: nephew; daughter: niece
Son's wife: daughter-in-law
Wife's/husband's brother: brother-in-law
Only daughter of my mother (said by a woman): herself

cards.title: Gender may be unknown
cards.body: If a person's gender is never stated, you **cannot** call them son or daughter; the answer is 'child', 'grandchild' or 'cannot be determined'. Examiners use this trap often.

cards.title: Coded relations
cards.body: If P + Q means 'P is father of Q' and P − Q means 'P is sister of Q', then A + B − C says A is B's father and B is C's sister, so A is **C's father** too.

cards.q: Pointing to a man, Riya says, 'His mother is the only daughter of my mother.' How is the man related to Riya?
cards.explain: The only daughter of Riya's mother is Riya herself, so the man's mother is Riya: he is her son.

cards.q: A is B's brother. C is A's mother. D is C's father. How is B related to D?
cards.explain: B is a child of C and therefore a grandchild of D, but B's gender is never given.

cards.q: P + Q: P is father of Q; P − Q: P is sister of Q. What does A + B − C mean for A and C?
cards.explain: A is B's father and B is C's sister, so A is C's father.

notes.p:
Blood-relation questions test whether you can turn words into a **family tree** without assuming anything. Draw as you read.

Use a simple notation: **+ for male, − for female**, a horizontal line or '=' for a married couple, and vertical lines for parent–child links. Keep each **generation on one level**. This makes questions like 'How is X related to Y?' a matter of counting levels.
points: Same level: siblings, cousins, spouses, brothers/sisters-in-law.
One level up: parents, uncles, aunts, parents-in-law.
Two levels up: grandparents.
One level down: children, nephews, nieces.

notes.p:
Break long sentences from the **end**.

**Worked example 1:** Pointing to a man, Riya says, "He is the son of my grandfather's only son."
Step 1: 'my grandfather's only son' → Riya's father (the only son of her paternal grandfather).
Step 2: 'son of my father' → Riya's brother (it cannot be Riya herself, because the person pointed at is a man).
Answer: the man is Riya's **brother**.

**Worked example 2:** A is B's sister. C is B's mother. D is C's father. E is D's mother. How is A related to D?
A and B are siblings, so C is also A's mother. D is C's father, so D is A's grandfather. A is female → A is D's **granddaughter**. (E is A's great-grandmother.)

Codes such as A + B are decoded one link at a time.

**Worked example 3:** A + B means A is the father of B; A − B means A is the wife of B; A × B means A is the brother of B; A ÷ B means A is the daughter of B. If **P + Q × R ÷ S**, how is S related to Q?
Step 1: P + Q → P is Q's father.
Step 2: Q × R → Q is R's brother, so P is also R's father.
Step 3: R ÷ S → R is the daughter of S, so S is R's parent.
Step 4: P is R's father, so S must be R's **mother** (P's wife).
Answer: S is Q's **mother**.
Never assume gender from a name. 'B is A's child' does not tell you if B is a son or daughter. If a question needs gender that is not given, the answer may be **'cannot be determined'**.
points: 'Sister', 'mother', 'wife', 'daughter' → female.
'Brother', 'father', 'husband', 'son' → male.
'Child', 'sibling', 'parent', 'spouse', 'cousin' → gender unknown.
Mother's or father's brother = uncle; their sister = aunt.
Brother's wife or wife's/husband's sister = sister-in-law.

notes.p: Avoid these errors.
points: Assuming gender from names (Kiran, Shashi, Santosh can be any gender).
Reading 'only son' and forgetting it means the father in pointing questions.
Mixing up generations when the chain is long; draw it.
In coded questions, decoding left-to-right but linking the wrong pair.
Choosing a relation when the answer should be 'cannot be determined'.

notes.p: Key points.
points: Draw a tree: + male, − female, = couple.
One generation per level.
Break long sentences from the end.
Decode coded relations link by link.
Gender words vs gender-neutral words.
If gender is missing, consider 'cannot be determined'.

cards.title: Fix the compass
cards.body: Draw north at the top of your rough sheet. A **right turn** = 90° clockwise, a **left turn** = 90° anticlockwise. Track the facing direction after every turn before plotting the next distance.

cards.title: Distance tools
points: Shortest distance = √(x² + y²)
Net east–west and net north–south first, then Pythagoras

cards.title: Shadow questions
cards.body: Morning: sun in the **east**, shadow falls **west**. Evening: sun in the west, shadow falls **east**. At noon there is practically no shadow, so these questions use morning or evening.

cards.title: Final direction wording
cards.body: If the end point is 6 km north and 8 km east of the start, the direction is **north-east**. Read whether the question asks direction 'of the start from the end' (reverse it) or 'of the end from the start'.

cards.q: Ravi walks 6 km north, turns right and walks 8 km. Distance and direction from the start?
cards.explain: √(6² + 8²) = 10 km; he is north and east of the start, i.e. North-East.

cards.q: In the morning, a man's shadow falls to his right. Which direction is he facing?
cards.explain: Morning shadow points west. If west is on his right, he faces south.

cards.q: Facing east, a girl turns 90° clockwise and then 180°. Which direction does she face now?
cards.explain: East → 90° clockwise = South → 180° = North.

notes.p:
There are **four main directions** (N, E, S, W) and **four in-between** (NE, SE, SW, NW). Turning **right** means turning **90° clockwise**; turning **left** means 90° anticlockwise. Facing north, your right is east; facing south, your right is west; facing east, your right is south; facing west, your right is north.

Use a **coordinate method**: start at (0, 0), north is +y, east is +x. Update the position after each move and use **Pythagoras** for the straight-line distance.
points: Distance = √(x² + y²).
Direction from start: compare signs of x and y.

notes.p:
Ravi walks 10 km north, turns right and walks 4 km, turns right again and walks 16 km, then turns left and walks 4 km. How far and in which direction is he from the start?

Step 1: north 10 → (0, 10).
Step 2: facing north, right = east; 4 km → (4, 10).
Step 3: facing east, right = south; 16 km → (4, −6).
Step 4: facing south, left = east; 4 km → (8, −6).
Distance = √(8² + 6²) = √(64 + 36) = √100 = **10 km**.
x is positive (east) and y is negative (south) → he is **south-east** of the start.

The sun rises in the east, so in the **morning shadows fall to the west**; in the **evening they fall to the east**. At noon in India the shadow is very short (and roughly northward, since the sun is to the south for most of the year).

**Question:** In the morning, Amit's shadow falls exactly to his **right**. Which way is he facing?
Morning shadow → west. So his right is west. A person whose right hand is west is facing **south**.
Check: facing south, right = west ✓.

A man faces north. He turns 135° clockwise and then 180° anticlockwise. Which direction is he facing now?

Net turn = 135° clockwise − 180° = **45° anticlockwise**.
45° anticlockwise from north = **north-west**.
Check step by step: north + 135° clockwise = south-east; south-east turned 180° = north-west ✓.

Useful rule: convert all turns into one direction (clockwise positive), add them, and reduce by 360° if needed.
These errors are frequent.
points: Turning right relative to the map, not relative to the person's current facing.
Forgetting that the final direction is from the start to the end point (not the reverse).
Mixing up 'the start is in which direction from him' (reverse direction).
Shadow questions asked about evening instead of morning.
Not simplifying net turns above 360°.

notes.p: Remember these.
points: Right = clockwise 90°, left = anticlockwise 90°.
Use coordinates: N = +y, E = +x.
Distance by Pythagoras; learn common triples.
Morning shadow west; evening shadow east.
Net turn = sum of clockwise turns − anticlockwise turns.
Read whether the question asks direction of end from start or start from end.

cards.title: Letter positions
points: Opposite letter: positions add to 27 (A↔Z, M↔N, R↔I)
Reverse position = 27 − forward position

cards.title: Common coding types
cards.body: **Shift** (+1, −2 each letter), **reverse** (opposite letters), **position sum** (word = sum of letter values), **mixed** (letters reversed then shifted), and **sentence coding** where whole words get codes.

cards.title: Sentence coding trick
cards.body: Compare two sentences that share one word: the code common to both is that word. Repeat with other pairs. Write the decoded words in a small table so you do not repeat work.

cards.title: Worked example
cards.body: BANK → CBOL. Each letter moves +1 (B→C, A→B, N→O, K→L). So LOAN → **MPBO**.

cards.q: If CAT = 24 (sum of letter positions), DOG = ?
BANK is coded as CBOL. How is LOAN coded?
cards.explain: Each letter shifts +1: L→M, O→P, A→B, N→O.

cards.q: What is the opposite letter of R (A↔Z pairing)?

notes.p: Coding–decoding checks whether you can find a rule that converts a word into a code. Common types are **letter shifting**, **opposite letters**, **position-value coding**, **sentence (word-group) coding** and **symbol coding with conditions** (common in Mains).
points: Positions: A = 1 … Z = 26. Learn **EJOTY = 5, 10, 15, 20, 25**.
**Opposite pairs** add up to 27: A–Z, B–Y, C–X, M–N.
Reverse position = 27 − position (G = 7 → 20 = T).

notes.p:
**Worked example 1 (shift):** COLD is written as DPME. How is WARM written?
C → D (+1), O → P (+1), L → M (+1), D → E (+1). Rule: each letter +1.
WARM → W+1 = X, A+1 = B, R+1 = S, M+1 = N → **XBSN**.

**Worked example 2 (opposite):** GIVE is coded as TREV. How is TAKE coded?
Find the rule: G (7) → 27 − 7 = 20 = T; I (9) → 18 = R; V (22) → 5 = E; E (5) → 22 = V. Rule: each letter is replaced by its **opposite letter**.
TAKE: T (20) → 7 = G; A (1) → 26 = Z; K (11) → 16 = P; E (5) → 22 = V → **GZPV**.

Several sentences are coded, word order is jumbled. Find the code of a word by locating it in two sentences and taking the **common code**.

**Worked example 3:**
'sky is blue' → 'ka to pa'
'blue sea water' → 'ne pa ri'
'water is cold' → 'ri to mo'
Step 1: 'blue' is in sentences 1 and 2; common code = **pa**.
Step 2: 'is' is in 1 and 3; common = **to**.
Step 3: 'water' is in 2 and 3; common = **ri**.
Step 4: leftovers: sentence 1 → sky = **ka**; sentence 2 → sea = **ne**; sentence 3 → cold = **mo**.

**Worked example 4 (position sum):** If BANK = 28, what is LOAN?
B 2 + A 1 + N 14 + K 11 = 28 ✓ (rule: sum of positions).
LOAN = L 12 + O 15 + A 1 + N 14 = **42**.

**Condition-based coding** gives a letter–symbol table plus rules like 'if the first letter is a vowel and the last a consonant, interchange their codes'. Check conditions **in the order given** and apply only the first one that matches, unless told otherwise.
points: Write the table once and mark vowels clearly.
Test each condition carefully; one wrong condition spoils all answers.

notes.p: Watch out for these.
points: Assuming a constant shift when it actually alternates (+1, −1, +1 …).
Forgetting that the code may be written in reverse order.
In sentence coding, guessing a word from only one sentence.
Applying two conditions when only the first applicable one counts.
Counting letter positions slowly; use EJOTY as anchors.

notes.p: Facts to memorise.
points: Opposite letter: 27 − position.
Check shift pattern on all letters, not one.
Sentence coding: common word ↔ common code.
Position sums and products are common number codes.
Condition coding: apply conditions in order.

cards.title: What it tests
cards.body: A 'machine' rearranges words and/or numbers step by step. You are shown the input and some steps, then asked for a later step, the last step, or the position of an element. Mostly a mains topic for SBI/IBPS PO.

cards.title: Find the rule from Step I and the last step
cards.body: Compare the input with Step I to see what moved, then check the final step: is it sorted ascending, descending or alphabetically? Usually one word and/or one number is placed per step from the left or right end.

cards.title: Common rules
cards.body: Sorting (alphabetical, by number of letters, ascending/descending), shifting (elements moved to an end), and arithmetic changes (add digits, square, multiply). Newer patterns combine a sort with an operation in the same step.

cards.title: Worked example
cards.body:
Rule: each step, the smallest remaining number moves to the left end of the unsorted part.
Input: 45 12 78 33
Step I: 12 45 78 33
Step II: 12 33 45 78 → sorted, so **2 steps**.

cards.q: Using the rule above (smallest remaining number moves left each step), how many steps does 45 12 78 33 need?
cards.explain: Step I places 12 and Step II places 33; 45 and 78 are then already in order.

cards.q: What is the best first move in an input–output question?
options: Guess the rule from the input alone
Compare the input with Step I and the last step
Solve the question for the last step first
Count the letters in each word
cards.explain: Comparing input → Step I → last step reveals both the movement and the final arrangement.

notes.p: A 'machine' rearranges a line of words and numbers step by step. You are shown an input and all steps for one example, then asked about another input. Questions ask for a particular step, the position of an element, or the number of steps. A set usually has **5 questions**, so cracking the rule is worth it.
points: **Shifting type:** one or two elements move to the ends each step.
**Arrangement/interchange type:** elements swap positions.
**Mathematical type:** numbers change by a rule (×2, +3, digit sum).

notes.p: Find the rule using the example, then run the machine on the new input.
points: Step 1: compare the **input and the last step** to see the final order (alphabetical? ascending?).
Step 2: compare **Step I with the input** to see which elements moved and to where.
Step 3: check whether words and numbers are handled separately.
Step 4: note how many elements move per step; the number of steps follows from that.
Step 5: apply the rule to the new input and write each step completely.

notes.p:
Rule (found from the example): in each step, the word that comes **first alphabetically** moves to the **left**, next to words already arranged; the **largest number** moves to the **right**, next to numbers already arranged.

Input: 39 power 17 jump 52 at 28 sky
Words in order: at, jump, power, sky. Numbers descending: 52, 39, 28, 17.
**Step I:** at 39 power 17 jump 28 sky 52
**Step II:** at jump power 17 28 sky 39 52
**Step III:** at jump power 17 sky 28 39 52
**Step IV:** at jump power sky 17 28 39 52
The arrangement is complete in **4 steps** (four word–number pairs).

**Question:** Which element is third from the right in Step II?
Step II from right: 52 (1st), 39 (2nd), **sky (3rd)**.

Rule: if a number is **even**, divide it by 2; if **odd**, add 1.

Input: 24 15 36 7
**Step I:** 24 → 12; 15 → 16; 36 → 18; 7 → 8 → **12 16 18 8**
**Step II:** 12 → 6; 16 → 8; 18 → 9; 8 → 4 → **6 8 9 4**
**Step III:** 6 → 3; 8 → 4; 9 → 10; 4 → 2 → **3 4 10 2**
Sum of Step III = 3 + 4 + 10 + 2 = **19**.

Write each step fully; questions often ask about a middle step.
Be careful about these.
points: Assuming the machine works like the last question you practised; always derive the rule.
Losing the relative order of unmoved elements when shifting.
Miscounting steps when the last step arranges two elements at once.
Answering 'from the left' when the question says 'from the right'.
Doing arithmetic in your head for mathematical machines; write it.

notes.p: Key ideas.
points: Compare input with last step to see the final order.
Compare input with Step I to see the movement rule.
Unmoved elements keep their relative order.
Write every step; questions target middle steps.
Count steps carefully at the end.
Skip this set in the exam if the rule is unclear within 2 minutes.

cards.title: What you decide
cards.body: You do **not** find the answer; you decide whether the given statements are **enough** to find it. Standard options: I alone, II alone, either alone, both together, or neither.

cards.title: Fixed order of checking
cards.body: 1) Check statement I alone. 2) Check II alone. 3) Only if both fail, combine them. Never combine first: if I alone is enough, 'both together' is wrong even though it also works.

cards.title: Unique answer needed
cards.body: Data is sufficient only if it gives **one definite answer**. If a puzzle can still be arranged in two ways, or a value can be ±, the data is insufficient (except in yes/no questions where both cases give the same answer).

cards.title: Worked example
cards.body:
Who is the tallest of P, Q, R?
I. P is taller than Q. II. R is taller than P.
I alone: R unknown. II alone: Q unknown. Together: R > P > Q, so **R is tallest** → both statements together are needed.

cards.q: What is A's age? I. A is 5 years older than B. II. B is 20 years old.
cards.explain: Neither statement alone gives A's age; together A = 20 + 5 = 25.

cards.q: x is an integer. Is x even? I. x² is even. II. 3x is even.
cards.explain: For an integer, x² even ⇒ x even, and 3x even ⇒ x even. Each statement alone answers it.

notes.p: You get a question and two (sometimes three) statements. You do **not** need the final answer; you only decide which statements are **enough to find a unique answer**. Standard options:
points: (a) Statement I alone is sufficient.
(b) Statement II alone is sufficient.
(c) Either I alone or II alone is sufficient.
(d) Both I and II together are needed.
(e) Even I and II together are not sufficient.

notes.p:
Always test the statements **independently first**, then together.

Step 1: check I alone. Step 2: forget I and check II alone. Step 3: only if neither works alone, combine them. A 'No' answer is still a definite answer: if a statement proves the number is **not** divisible by 6, it is sufficient.

Stop calculating once you know the answer is unique; full computation wastes time.

**Example 1 (reasoning):** Who is the tallest among P, Q and R?
I. P is taller than Q. II. R is taller than P.
I alone: R unknown → no. II alone: Q unknown → no.
Together: R > P > Q → R is tallest → **(d) both needed**.

**Example 2 (quant):** What is the cost price of an article?
I. It was sold for ₹600 at a 20% profit. II. The profit was ₹100.
I alone: CP = 600 ÷ 1.2 = ₹500 → sufficient.
II alone: profit amount without SP or % → not sufficient.
Answer: **(a)**.

**Example 3:** What is the area of a square?
I. Its side is 8 cm. II. Its diagonal is 8√2 cm.
I → 64 cm². II → side = diagonal/√2 = 8 → 64 cm². Each works alone → **(c) either**.

**Example 4:** What is the value of x?
I. x² = 49. II. x > 0.
I gives ±7 (not unique). II alone gives nothing. Together → x = 7 → **(d)**.
These are set on purpose.
points: Carrying information from Statement I into your check of Statement II.
Treating two possible values as 'sufficient'.
Using outside assumptions (e.g. assuming a person is male).
Thinking a 'No' answer means insufficient.
Choosing (d) when one statement alone was already enough.

notes.p:
Some questions give three statements and ask which **combination** is enough. Check single statements first, then pairs.

**Worked example:** What is R's age?
I. R is 5 years older than S. II. The sum of R's and S's ages is 45. III. S is 20 years old.
Alone: none gives R's age.
I + II: R − S = 5 and R + S = 45 → 2R = 50 → R = **25**.
I + III: R = 20 + 5 = **25**.
II + III: R = 45 − 20 = **25**.
Answer: **any two statements together are sufficient**.
Remember:
points: Sufficient = unique answer, not necessarily 'yes'.
Check I alone, II alone, then together.
Never mix statements during the single checks.
Stop once uniqueness is clear.
x² = k gives two values unless a sign is fixed.
Both statements giving the same info separately → 'either'.

cards.title: Facing decides left and right
cards.body: Facing **north** (towards you reading the page from below), the person’s right is your right. Facing **south**, their right is your **left**. Always draw the row and mark the facing direction first.

cards.title: Key phrases
cards.body: "Immediate right" = adjacent seat. "Second to the right" = skip one seat. "Sits at an extreme end" = position 1 or n. "Two persons sit between" = gap of 3 positions.

cards.title: Double row
cards.body: Two parallel rows face each other (Row 1 faces south, Row 2 north). Each person has an **opposite** in the other row; left-right flips between rows.

cards.title: Square/rectangular tables
cards.body: People at **corners** often face the centre; those at **middle of sides** may face outside. Facing centre: left = clockwise. Facing outside: left = anticlockwise.

cards.title: Start with fixed clues
cards.body: Begin with clues that pin an absolute position (end, middle, opposite). Then use relative clues. When a clue gives two options, draw both cases and kill one with the next clue.

cards.q: Five people sit in a row facing north. C is in the middle; A is second to the left of C; B is immediately right of C; E is not at an end. Who is at the right end?
cards.explain: Positions: A1, E2, C3, B4, so D5.

cards.q: People face south. "X is to the right of Y" means that on the page X appears:
cards.explain: Facing south, their right is the reader’s left.

cards.q: In a row of 8 facing north, how many sit between the 2nd from the left and the 3rd from the right?
cards.explain: Positions 2 and 6; seats 3, 4, 5 lie between.

notes.p: Seating arrangement and puzzles carry the largest weight in bank reasoning: in Mains, often more than half of the section. Linear rows, double rows and square/rectangular tables share one method — fix positions with absolute clues, then fill relative clues, branching into cases when needed.

Number seats 1 to n from left to right on your page. If everyone faces **north**, "right" means a higher seat number. If everyone faces **south**, "right" means a lower seat number. If facing is mixed, mark each person with an arrow (↑ or ↓) and apply their own left/right.

Gap language: "**two persons** sit between A and B" means |positions| differ by **3**. "A sits **third to the left** of B" means A is 3 seats away to B’s left.

Six people L, M, N, O, P, Q sit in a row facing north.
1. N sits at the left end.
2. Two people sit between N and P.
3. Q sits immediately right of P.
4. O sits at an extreme end.
5. L sits to the left of M.

Step 1: N = 1. Step 2: P = 4. Step 3: Q = 5. Step 4: left end is taken, so O = 6. Step 5: seats 2 and 3 remain for L and M; L is left of M → L = 2, M = 3.
Final: **N L M P Q O**. Who sits between M and Q? **P**.

Two rows of equal length face each other. Row 1 (top) faces south, Row 2 (bottom) faces north, unless stated otherwise. Clues such as "A faces the person who sits second to the right of B" link the rows.

Tip: draw both rows on the same columns. A person in Row 1 at column 3 faces the Row 2 person at column 3. Because the rows face opposite ways, "right" in Row 1 is towards a lower column on your page, and "right" in Row 2 is towards a higher column.

Typical setup: 8 people, 4 at corners and 4 at the middle of the sides. Corner people may face the centre; middle-side people may face outward (or vice versa).

**Worked example 2:** Four people sit at the corners of a square table facing the centre: A, B, C, D. A is to the immediate left of B; C is not adjacent to A. Facing centre, left is clockwise. Place B at top-left; A is then clockwise from B at top-right. C is not adjacent to A, so C must be diagonally opposite at bottom-left. D takes bottom-right. D is therefore **opposite B**.
points: Facing centre: left = clockwise, right = anticlockwise.
Facing outside: reverse both.

notes.p: Errors that cost marks.
points: Applying north-facing rules to south-facing people.
Reading "two persons between" as a gap of 2.
Dropping a valid case too early.
Not re-checking all clues on the final arrangement.

notes.p: Seating rules.
points: Facing north: right = right on page; south: reversed.
"n persons between" → gap of n + 1.
Fix absolute clues first.
Branch into cases; eliminate with later clues.
Facing centre: left = clockwise.
Verify the final arrangement against every clue.

cards.title: Facing centre
cards.body: Around a circle facing the centre, **left = clockwise** and **right = anticlockwise**. Facing outside, both reverse. Some questions mix facing; mark each person.

cards.title: Opposite seats
cards.body: With an even number n of seats, each person has one opposite. In a circle of 8, **3 people** sit between two opposite persons on each side.

cards.title: Converse relations
cards.body: If X is second to the right of Y, then Y is second to the **left** of X. Use this to read clues from either person’s point of view.

cards.title: Placing a clue
cards.body: Six seats numbered 0–5 clockwise, all facing centre. R at 0. "P is second to the left of R" → move 2 seats clockwise → P at 2.

cards.title: Fix one person
cards.body: Rotation does not change a circular arrangement, so fix the first well-connected person at the top and build around them. This removes one whole set of cases.

cards.q: Facing the centre, "A is to the immediate left of B" means A sits next to B in which direction?
cards.explain: Facing centre, left is clockwise.

cards.q: In a circle of 8 people, how many sit between two people who are opposite each other (counting one side)?
cards.explain: 8 seats: 3 on each side between opposite seats.

cards.q: In a circle facing the centre, X is second to the right of Y. Then Y is ____ of X.
cards.explain: Relations reverse when you switch the reference person.

notes.p:
Circular arrangements appear alone (6–8 people) or combined with other attributes (cities, professions, colours). Sometimes some people face the centre and some face outside, which is the main source of errors.

Direction rules: when facing the **centre**, a person’s left lies **clockwise** and right **anticlockwise**. When facing **outside**, left is anticlockwise and right is clockwise.

Six friends P, Q, R, S, T, U sit around a circular table facing the centre.
1. P sits second to the left of R.
2. S sits opposite P.
3. T sits immediately right of S.
4. Q is not adjacent to R.

Number seats 0–5 clockwise; put R at 0.
Clue 1: left = clockwise → P at 2.
Clue 2: opposite of 2 is 5 → S at 5.
Clue 3: right = anticlockwise → T at 4.
Seats 1 and 3 remain for Q and U. Seat 1 is adjacent to R, so Q = 3, U = 1.
Final (clockwise): **R, U, P, Q, T, S**. Who sits between P and T? **Q**.

Four people sit around a circle: A and C face the centre, B and D face outside. A is opposite C. B sits to the immediate right of A. Place A at the top (seat 0) of a 4-seat circle; C is at seat 2. A faces centre, so A’s right is anticlockwise → B at seat 3. D takes seat 1. D faces outside; D’s right is clockwise → seat 2 → **C is to D’s immediate right**.
points: Mark ↑ (centre) or ↓ (outside) next to every person before reading the questions.

notes.p:
Clues like "A sits third to the left of B" fix a seat, but "A and B are neighbours" gives two options. Keep both cases on paper; a later clue usually removes one. If two cases survive all clues, the question will ask only about something that is the same in both — otherwise the answer is "cannot be determined".

Circles may also be combined with **attributes**: each person likes a different fruit or works in a different city. Build the seating first, then use a separate column for the attribute. Questions such as "Which of the following pairs is not adjacent?" or "Four of five pairs are alike in a certain way" are answered by checking each option against the final diagram — never by memory.
Avoid these.
points: Using north-south (linear) rules in a circle.
Forgetting to reverse directions for outside-facing people.
Counting opposite seats wrongly in odd-sized circles (there is no exact opposite).
Fixing two people before checking their relation.

notes.p: Circle essentials.
points: Facing centre: left = clockwise.
Facing outside: left = anticlockwise.
Fix one person; rotation does not matter.
In 8 seats, opposite persons have 3 between them on each side.
Converse: right of ↔ left of.
Keep both cases until a clue kills one.

cards.title: Vertical puzzles
cards.body: In **floor** and **box** puzzles, positions run bottom to top (floor 1 = lowest) unless stated. "Above" means any higher floor; "immediately above" means the next floor.

cards.title: Scheduling puzzles
cards.body: People or events are placed on **days, weeks, months or years**. Know the order of months and which have 31 days (Jan, Mar, May, Jul, Aug, Oct, Dec).

cards.title: Gap language
points: "One person between A and B" → positions differ by 2
"Two persons between" → differ by 3
"Above/below" without "immediately" → any distance
Months: 30 days in Apr, Jun, Sep, Nov; Feb 28/29

cards.title: Floor puzzle in brief
cards.body:
5 floors. E on floor 1; B on an even floor; two people between B and D; C immediately above A.
B = 2 → D = 5; A = 3, C = 4. (B = 4 → D = 1, taken.)

cards.title: Table with attributes
cards.body: Draw a table: floors (or days) as rows, columns for person, colour, city… Fill absolute clues, then mark crosses (✗) for impossible combinations.

cards.q: In a 7-floor building (floor 1 at the bottom), how many floors are above floor 3?
cards.explain: Floors 4, 5, 6, 7.

cards.q: In an 8-floor building, X lives on floor 6 and two persons live between X and Y. Y lives on floor:
cards.explain: Gap of 3: floor 3 (floor 9 does not exist).

cards.q: How many months of the year have 31 days?
cards.explain: Jan, Mar, May, Jul, Aug, Oct, Dec.

notes.p: Floor, box and scheduling puzzles are the **most frequent** Mains puzzle types in SBI and IBPS. They work like a vertical linear arrangement, often with a second attribute (flat type, colour, company). The skill is organising information so that each new clue removes possibilities.

Five people A, B, C, D, E live on floors 1–5 (1 = bottom), one per floor.
1. E lives on floor 1.
2. B lives on an even-numbered floor.
3. Two people live between B and D.
4. C lives immediately above A.

Clue 2 gives B = 2 or 4.
If B = 4, clue 3 gives D = 1 — taken by E. ✗
So B = 2, D = 5.
Floors 3 and 4 remain; C is immediately above A → **A = 3, C = 4**.
Final: 1 E, 2 B, 3 A, 4 C, 5 D.

P, Q, R, S, T attend training on different days from Monday to Friday.
1. R attends on Wednesday.
2. Q attends the day after R.
3. Two people attend between P and T.
4. T does not attend on Friday.

R = Wed, Q = Thu. Remaining: Mon, Tue, Fri for P, S, T.
Two people between P and T → the pair must be (Mon, Thu) or (Tue, Fri). Thu is taken, so {P, T} = {Tue, Fri}.
T is not on Friday → **T = Tue, P = Fri**, S = Mon.
Final: S, T, R, Q, P.

Boxes are stacked one above another, often with an attribute such as colour or number of items. Clues like "as many boxes above X as below Y" need care: count the boxes, not the positions. With 7 boxes, a box with 2 boxes above it is box 5 from the bottom.

In month/year-based scheduling ("born in different years"), convert ages to years and remember the reference year given in the question.

**Floor + flat puzzles:** a building may have floors 1–4 and two flats on each floor (Flat A to the west of Flat B). Draw a grid with floors as rows and flats as columns. A clue such as "P lives directly above Q’s flat" fixes the same column on the next floor up. Such grid puzzles are common in Mains and reward a neat diagram.
points: Mark an impossible cell with ✗ immediately — elimination is faster than placement.
Write "case 1 / case 2" side by side.

notes.p: Avoid these.
points: Treating "above" as "immediately above".
Numbering floors from the top when the question numbers from the bottom.
Assuming every month has 30 days.
Forgetting that "between" excludes the two people named.

notes.p: Checklist.
points: Floor 1 = bottom unless stated.
Gap language: n between → difference n + 1.
31-day months: Jan, Mar, May, Jul, Aug, Oct, Dec.
Draw a table; fill absolute clues first.
Branch into cases; eliminate quickly.
Re-verify all clues at the end.

cards.title: Position formulas
points: Total = rank from left + rank from right − 1
Rank from other end = total − rank + 1
Persons between two positions = difference − 1
After interchange: new position gives the other person’s old position

cards.title: Comparison ranking
cards.body: Statements like "P is taller than Q but shorter than R" create a chain. Write symbols: R > P > Q. Merge chains and read off tallest, shortest or nth.

cards.title: Total in a row
cards.body:
Ravi is 12th from the left and 18th from the right.
Total = 12 + 18 − 1 = **29**.

cards.title: Minimum and maximum
cards.body: When the relative order of two people is not given, consider both cases (A before B, B before A). One gives the maximum total, the other the minimum.

cards.title: Draw a line
cards.body: Draw a horizontal line, mark the left and right ends and the known positions. Most errors come from computing in the head.

cards.q: In a class of 40, Asha is 15th from the top. Her rank from the bottom is:
In a row of 40, A is 10th from the left and B is 15th from the right. How many people sit between them?
cards.explain: B from left = 26; between = 26 − 10 − 1 = 15.

cards.q: P is taller than Q but shorter than R. S is the tallest and T is shorter than Q. Who is second shortest?
cards.explain: Order: S > R > P > Q > T.

notes.p:
Order and ranking questions ask for positions in a row or queue, ranks in a class, or comparisons of height, weight or marks. They appear directly in Prelims and are embedded in puzzles. Two formulas solve almost all of them.

**Total = left rank + right rank − 1.** Someone 5th from the left and 5th from the right in the same row is in a row of 9.

When two people swap places, each takes the other’s position.

**Worked example 1:** In a row, A is 12th from the left and B is 18th from the right. They interchange; A is now 25th from the left. How many people are in the row?
A’s new position is B’s old position, which is 25th from the left and 18th from the right.
Total = 25 + 18 − 1 = **42**.

B’s new position is 12th from the left = 42 − 12 + 1 = 31st from the right.

**Worked example 2:** In a queue, A is 5th from the front and B is 8th from the end. Three people stand between them. Find the minimum and maximum number in the queue.
Case 1 (A ahead of B): A = 5, B = 9; B is 8th from the end → total = 9 + 8 − 1 = **16**.
Case 2 (B ahead of A): B = 1, A = 5; B is 8th from the end → total = 1 + 8 − 1 = **8**.
Check case 2: positions 2, 3, 4 lie between ✓.
Minimum 8, maximum 16.

**Worked example 3:** Among five students, M scored more than N but less than O. P scored the least. Q scored more than O. Order: Q > O > M > N > P. Third highest = **M**.

If a statement leaves two possibilities ("L is shorter than K" with no other link), mark both, and answer "cannot be determined" if the question depends on them.

For **numerical comparisons** ("the second tallest is 165 cm, A is 5 cm shorter than the tallest"), first build the order chain, then attach numbers. Questions may ask for possible values within a range; check which options fit between the neighbouring values.
points: Write > or < chains; never hold them in memory.
A person ranked nth from top among n people is also last.

notes.p: Avoid these.
points: Forgetting to subtract 1 in the total formula.
Counting the two named people in "between".
Missing the overlap case in min/max questions.
Mixing "from the top" and "from the bottom".

notes.p: Ranking formulas.
points: Total = L + R − 1.
Other-end rank = total − rank + 1.
Between = difference − 1.
Interchange: the new position belongs to the other person’s old position.
Min/max: try both orders.
Build > chains for comparisons.

cards.title: Letter positions
points: Position from the right = 27 − position from the left
Opposite pairs add to 27: A–Z, B–Y, M–N

cards.title: Alphanumeric series
cards.body: A string of letters, digits and symbols is given. Questions ask what is "nth to the right of the mth from the left", or how many elements satisfy a condition ("number immediately followed by a symbol").

cards.title: Direction rule
points: Nth to the right of the mth from the left = (m + n)th from the left
Nth to the left of the mth from the left = (m − n)th from the left
Mth from the right in a string of L = (L − m + 1)th from the left

cards.title: Number the string
cards.body: Write position numbers above the string once. Every later question then becomes arithmetic, not recounting.

cards.q: The 15th letter of the English alphabet from the left is:
cards.explain: EJOTY: O = 15.

cards.q: A, C, F, J, O, ?
In "B 3 # K 7 @ 5 M % 2 Q", how many numbers are immediately followed by a symbol?
cards.explain: 3# and 7@ qualify; 5M and 2Q do not.

notes.p:
Bank reasoning has two closely related question types: **letter series** (find the next letters by a gap pattern) and **alphanumeric series** (a mixed string of letters, numbers and symbols with position or condition questions). Both depend on fast letter-position recall.

Memorise **EJOTY** (5, 10, 15, 20, 25) and use it as anchors: R is 3 after O (15): P 16, Q 17, **R 18**. W is 2 before Y (25) → **23**. Counting from the nearest anchor is faster than counting from A.

String (16 elements): 7 R # 4 T @ K 2 $ M 9 % P 3 & Z
Number them 1–16.

(a) Which element is 5th to the right of the 4th from the left?
4 + 5 = 9th from left → **$**.

(b) Which element is 3rd to the left of the 6th from the right?
6th from right = 16 − 6 + 1 = 11th from left; 3rd to its left = 8th → **2**.

Same string. How many letters are immediately preceded by a number?
Letters: R (after 7 ✓), T (after 4 ✓), K (after @), M (after $), P (after %), Z (after &).
Answer: **2**.

If all symbols are removed, which element is 6th from the right?
New string: 7 R 4 T K 2 M 9 P 3 Z (11 elements). 6th from right = 11 − 6 + 1 = 6th from left → **2**.
points: Read the condition word by word: "immediately preceded by a number and followed by a symbol" needs both checks.

notes.p:
Common patterns: constant gaps (B, E, H, K → +3), increasing gaps (A, B, D, G, K → +1, +2, +3, +4), alternate series (A, Z, B, Y, C, X), and grouped letters (AZ, BY, CX — opposite pairs).

**Worked example 3:** Z, W, S, N, ? → gaps −3, −4, −5 → −6 → **H** (N = 14, 14 − 6 = 8 = H).

**Word-based letter questions:** "How many pairs of letters in the word MOBILE have as many letters between them in the word as in the alphabet?" Write positions (M 13, O 15, B 2, I 9, L 12, E 5) and check every pair. O and L have two letters between them in the word (B, I) and two in the alphabet (M, N) → a pair. B and E have two between in the word (I, L) and two in the alphabet (C, D) → a pair. No other pair works, so the answer is **2**. Work systematically from the first letter so no pair is missed.
Avoid these.
points: Counting the starting element when moving "nth to the right".
Using the original string after the question removes symbols.
Confusing left/right ends after reversing a string.
Miscounting letters far from anchors — use EJOTY.

notes.p: Series essentials.
points: Opposite letters sum to 27.
Right of mth from left: m + n; left: m − n.
mth from right = L − m + 1 from left.
Number the string once.
Re-number if elements are removed.

cards.title: What changed
cards.body: Recent Mains papers use **multi-step letter coding** (reverse, then shift), **position-value coding** (letters to numbers), **conditional coding** of digits/symbols, and **sentence coding** with word-length or letter clues.

cards.title: Reverse and shift
cards.body:
BANK → reverse KNAB → each +1 → **LOBC**.
So CASH → HSAC → **ITBD**.

cards.title: Common operations
points: Shift: +n / −n positions; opposite letter (27 − n)
Reverse whole word or halves
Vowels and consonants treated differently
Number codes: sum, product or digit-wise positions
Word code = f(first letter, last letter, length)

cards.title: Sentence coding
cards.body: Compare sentences that share a word; the common code is that word’s code. Repeat until each word is fixed. In new patterns, check whether the code depends on the word’s letters (e.g. number of letters).

cards.title: Test on two words
cards.body: Find the rule on one word, then confirm it on a second before applying it. Many options are built from a plausible but wrong rule.

cards.q: If BANK is coded LOBC (reverse, then +1), CASH is coded:
cards.explain: CASH → HSAC → ITBD.

cards.q: If CAT = 24 (sum of letter positions), DOG = ?
Each vowel is replaced by the next letter and each consonant by the previous letter. MILK becomes:
cards.explain: M→L, I→J, L→K, K→J.

notes.p:
Classic coding (shift every letter by 1) is now rare in Mains. Examiners combine two or three operations, or tie the code to a property of the word, so you must test rules systematically. Prelims still has the simpler forms.

A typical Mains set gives 3–4 coded examples and 5 questions. Spend the first minute decoding the rule completely; the questions then take seconds each. Partial understanding leads to errors in every question of the set.

**Worked example 1:** In a code, PAPER is written as SFQBQ. Find the code for TABLE.
Reverse PAPER → REPAP; shift each letter +1 → SFQBQ ✓.
TABLE → reverse ELBAT → +1 → **FMCBU**.

Always check whether the reverse comes before or after the shift — for +1 it gives the same result, but for position-dependent shifts (+1, +2, +3…) it does not.

Letters become numbers through position values.

**Worked example 2:** If BAD = 7 (2 + 1 + 4), then FACE = 6 + 1 + 3 + 5 = **15**.

**Worked example 3:** If ROSE = 6821 and CHAIR = 73456, find SEARCH.
From ROSE: R = 6, O = 8, S = 2, E = 1. From CHAIR: C = 7, H = 3, A = 4, I = 5, R = 6 ✓ (consistent).
SEARCH → S 2, E 1, A 4, R 6, C 7, H 3 → **214673**.

**Worked example 4:**
"sky is blue" → "la pa ta"
"blue water" → "ta ri"
"water is cool" → "ri pa so"
blue = common of 1 and 2 = **ta**; is = common of 1 and 3 = **pa**; water = **ri**; sky = **la**; cool = **so**.

New-pattern variant: each word coded as (last letter)(number of letters)(first letter + 1). TRAIN → N5U; BANK → K4C. Test the rule on every given word before decoding a new one.

Digits are coded as symbols with conditions such as "If the first digit is even and the last is odd, their codes are interchanged". Apply conditions in the order given and stop at the first one that applies (unless the question says otherwise). Write the code under each digit before checking conditions.
points: Read every condition before coding.
If none applies, code digit by digit.

notes.p: Avoid these.
points: Applying the rule to only one sample word.
Reversing after shifting when the order matters.
Assuming codes keep the word order in sentence coding.
Missing the "none of the conditions apply" case.

notes.p: Coding toolkit.
points: Check reverse, shift, opposite letters.
Vowels/consonants may change differently.
Position values: A = 1 … Z = 26.
Sentence coding: common words ↔ common codes.
Conditional coding: apply conditions in order.
Verify the rule on a second example.

cards.title: Assumption
cards.body: An **assumption** is something the speaker takes for granted without stating it. It is implicit if the statement would not make sense without it.

cards.title: Negation test
cards.body: Negate the assumption. If the statement then becomes pointless or illogical, the assumption is **implicit**. "Advertise in the paper" assumes people read the paper; if nobody reads it, advertising there makes no sense.

cards.title: Strong argument
cards.body: A **strong argument** is relevant to the question, addresses an important aspect, and is backed by a reason or consequence. Arguments based on popularity, emotion, ideal situations or very general claims are **weak**.

cards.title: Words that weaken
cards.body: Extreme words — **only, all, always, never, best** — usually make an assumption or argument invalid unless the statement itself is extreme.

cards.title: Assumption example
cards.body: "Open an account with Bank X and get free insurance." Implicit: people value free insurance. Not implicit: other banks do not offer insurance (no comparison is made).

cards.q: Notice: "Use the stairs; the lift is under repair." Assumptions — I: People can read the notice. II: The lift will never be repaired.
cards.explain: A notice assumes it will be read; "under repair" implies it will be fixed.

cards.q: Should plastic bags be banned? I: Yes, they cause long-lasting pollution. II: No, everyone uses them.
cards.explain: I gives a real consequence; II is popularity, which is weak.

notes.p: Statement-based logical reasoning (assumptions, arguments, course of action, conclusions) appears in SBI and IBPS PO Mains and RBI Grade B Phase I, usually as 3–5 questions. The answer options are fixed: "only I", "only II", "either", "neither", "both". Practise judging each statement independently.

An assumption is an **unstated premise**. Ask: "What must the speaker believe for this statement to make sense?"

**Worked example 1:** Statement: "The government has decided to raise the tax on tobacco to reduce smoking."
I: Higher prices reduce consumption of tobacco to some extent. — **Implicit** (otherwise the policy makes no sense).
II: All smokers will quit. — **Not implicit** (too extreme).
Answer: **only I**.

Useful pointers: advice, appeals and notices assume they will be followed; actions assume the desired result is possible; "either I or II" applies when the two assumptions are complementary and together cover all cases.

A strong argument must be **relevant**, **important** and **supported**. Mark weak those that are:
- based on popularity ("everyone does it") or tradition,
- emotional or ideological without reasons,
- about an ideal world ("people should be honest"),
- trivial or merely restating the question.

**Worked example 2:** Should online classes replace school education? I: Yes, they save travel time. II: No, schools build social skills that online classes cannot.
I names a real but minor convenience; it does not address whether online classes can do what schools do, so it is weak for a question about **replacing** schools. II gives an important, specific reason tied to the question → **only II is strong**. (Different question-setters can judge borderline arguments differently; focus on relevance and importance.)

Read the question first, then each argument with three checks: Does it address the question? Is the reason important? Is it supported? For assumptions, apply the negation test in one line. Avoid adding outside knowledge; judge only what the statement implies.
points: Extreme words usually fail.
Comparisons not made in the statement are not assumed.

notes.p:
A related type gives a statement and asks which **conclusions** follow. A conclusion follows only if it is a necessary consequence of the statement, not merely plausible.

**Worked example 3:** Statement: "All the employees of the branch attended the training on cyber security."
I: The branch has employees. — Follows.
II: Employees of other branches did not attend. — Does not follow (nothing is said about them).
Answer: **only I**.

The same discipline applies across all statement types: judge only what the words commit the speaker to.
Avoid these.
points: Treating a fact you know as an assumption of the statement.
Calling an argument strong because you agree with it.
Missing "either I or II" cases.
Over-reading the statement.

notes.p: Rules.
points: Assumption = unstated but necessary.
Negation test.
Strong argument = relevant + important + supported.
Popularity, emotion, ideals → weak.
Extreme words → usually not implicit.
Judge only from the statement.

cards.title: Course of action
cards.body: A **course of action** follows if it is practical, addresses the problem (or reduces it) and is within the authority of whoever acts. Drastic, unrelated or impractical steps do not follow.

cards.title: Cause and effect
cards.body: Two events: decide whether A causes B, B causes A, both are independent causes, both result from a common cause, or both are independent effects. The **cause comes earlier** and logically produces the effect.

cards.title: Inferences
cards.body: Passage-based: mark each inference **definitely true**, **probably true**, **data inadequate**, **probably false** or **definitely false**. "Definitely" needs the passage itself; "probably" needs reasonable support.

cards.title: Strengthen / weaken
cards.body: A **strengthening** statement supplies evidence that the claim’s mechanism works; a **weakening** one shows an alternative cause or a reason the mechanism fails.

cards.title: Stay inside the text
cards.body: Use general knowledge only to understand words, never to add facts. Most wrong answers rely on information the passage does not give.

cards.q: Many dengue cases are reported in a locality. I: The municipality should clear stagnant water and fumigate. II: Residents should be asked to leave the city.
cards.explain: I tackles the cause practically; II is drastic.

cards.q: A: Vegetable prices rose sharply. B: Heavy rains damaged crops in growing regions.
options: A is the cause, B the effect
B is the cause, A the effect
Both are effects of a common cause
cards.explain: Crop damage reduces supply and raises prices.

cards.q: Claim: "The new metro line will cut road traffic in the city." Which statement strengthens it?
options: Most car commuters on that corridor say they will switch to the metro
Metro fares are higher than bus fares
The metro line opens next year
cards.explain: It shows the mechanism (car users switching) will work.

notes.p: These "critical reasoning" types test judgement rather than calculation. They appear in PO Mains, RBI Grade B and NABARD Phase I. Each option set is standard, so learn the decision rules and apply them consistently.

A course of action **follows** if it is (1) practical and feasible, (2) directed at solving, reducing or preventing the problem, and (3) proportionate.

**Worked example 1:** Statement: "Several students fell ill after eating at a school canteen."
I: The canteen’s food should be tested and the canteen inspected. — Follows (practical, relevant).
II: All school canteens in the state should be shut permanently. — Does not follow (drastic, disproportionate).
Answer: **only I**.

Long-term and short-term actions can both follow if each addresses the problem.

**Decision-making sets** (NABARD, some PO papers) give a rule — for example, applicants must be 21–35 years old and graduates; graduates over 35 with 5 years of banking experience are referred to the GM — and then candidate profiles. A 37-year-old graduate with 6 years in a bank → **refer to GM**; a 25-year-old without a degree → **not eligible**. Check each condition in order and note any the data does not mention ("data inadequate").

**Worked example 2:** A: The central bank raised interest rates. B: Inflation has stayed above target for several months.
B happened first and explains A → **B is the cause, A the effect**.

If both events stem from a third factor (A: Schools closed; B: Train services cancelled — both because of a cyclone), choose "**effects of a common cause**".

**Worked example 3:** Passage: "India’s services sector contributes over half of gross value added, while agriculture employs a large share of the workforce."
Inference: "Average output per worker is higher in services than in agriculture." — **Probably true** (strongly suggested by the shares, but not stated).
Inference: "Agriculture contributes more output than services." — **Definitely false** (contradicts the passage).
Inference: "Services exports grew last year." — **Data inadequate**.

For a claim "X will lead to Y", a **strengthener** shows the link from X to Y works (survey, past evidence). A **weakener** shows Y has another cause, or that X cannot produce Y. Statements about timing or unrelated facts are neutral.

**Worked example 4:** Claim: "Cutting the GST rate on two-wheelers will raise their sales." Weakener: "Most potential buyers delay purchases because of high loan interest rates, not price." It offers a different binding constraint, so the tax cut may not lift sales. Strengthener: "After the last rate cut, sales rose within two quarters."
points: Pick the option that affects the link, not one that merely mentions the topic.

notes.p: Avoid these.
points: Choosing drastic or unrelated actions because they "sound strict".
Reversing cause and effect.
Marking "definitely true" for well-supported guesses.
Using outside facts in inferences.

notes.p: Rules.
points: Course of action: practical, relevant, proportionate.
Cause precedes effect.
Common cause when both stem from a third event.
Definitely = stated; probably = supported; inadequate = no basis.
Strengthen/weaken: target the link.

cards.title: Biggest English block
cards.body: RC gives **8–10 questions** in prelims and more in mains. Passages are often on the economy, banking, technology and environment, so reading business news daily doubles as GA prep.

cards.title: Questions first, then passage
cards.body: Skim the questions first to know what to look for. Then read the passage once, actively, noting the **main idea of each paragraph** in two or three words. Go back only to the relevant paragraph for each question.

cards.title: Question types
points: Fact-based: answer is stated directly
Inference: what is implied but not stated
Main idea / title / tone of the author
Vocabulary: synonym/antonym in context

cards.title: Inference traps
cards.body: Reject options that are **too extreme** ('always', 'never'), out of scope, or true in general but not supported by the passage. The right inference is the one that must be true from the text.

cards.q: Passage: 'Digital payments have cut the cost of transactions, but they have also exposed first-time users to fraud. Financial literacy must therefore keep pace with technology.' The author's main point is:
options: Financial literacy must grow along with digital adoption
Fraud is the only result of digital payments
cards.explain: The last sentence ('therefore') states the conclusion: literacy must keep pace with technology.

cards.q: In RC, which option should usually be rejected first?
options: One with extreme words like 'always' or 'never'
cards.explain: Extreme words usually go beyond what the passage supports.

notes.p: Reading comprehension (RC) is usually the **biggest single block in English**: 7–10 questions in Prelims and more in Mains. Passages come from economy, banking, technology, environment and social issues, often adapted from editorials. RC rewards steady practice more than any trick, because speed and understanding grow with daily reading.
points: Read one editorial (The Hindu, Indian Express, Mint) every day.
Note 5 new words with their meaning in context.
Practise one timed RC (8–9 minutes) daily in the last two months.

notes.h: Question types and how to handle them
notes.p: Knowing the question type tells you where to look in the passage.
points: **Main idea / title:** think about the whole passage, not one paragraph.
**Specific detail:** scan for the keyword, then read 2 lines before and after.
**Inference:** the answer is not written directly but must be **logically implied**.
**Vocabulary in context:** choose the meaning that fits **this sentence**, not the dictionary's first meaning.
**Tone/attitude:** critical, analytical, optimistic, cautious, sarcastic.
**True/false/not stated:** check each statement against exact lines.

notes.h: A reading method that saves time
notes.p:
Step 1: glance at the questions (not the options) to know what to look for.
Step 2: read the passage once at a steady pace; note the **topic, the author's view and the structure** (problem → cause → solution).
Step 3: answer detail and vocabulary questions first, then inference and main-idea questions.
Step 4: eliminate options; at least two are usually clearly wrong.

**Worked example:** Passage line: "The bank cut its lending rate, hoping cheaper loans would revive demand. Yet borrowing barely rose, as households worried about job security."
Question: What can be inferred?
(A) Banks never cut rates. (B) Lower rates alone may not raise borrowing when confidence is weak. (C) Households had no jobs. (D) Demand rose sharply.
A and D contradict the text; C is an exaggeration ('worried about' ≠ 'had no jobs'). **B** follows logically → correct.

Words often have several meanings. In 'The committee will **address** the issue', address = deal with, not a postal address. Replace the word with each option and read the sentence; the correct option keeps the meaning unchanged.

For **synonym/antonym** questions, watch out for options that are related but not equal in strength (e.g. 'dislike' vs 'detest').
Examiners design wrong options around these.
points: **Extreme words**: always, never, only, completely; rarely correct in inference questions.
**Outside knowledge**: an option may be true in real life but not supported by the passage.
**Half-right options**: first half matches, second half distorts.
**Word-match traps**: copying exact words from the passage but changing the meaning.
Spending too long on one passage; move on after 9–10 minutes.

notes.p: Before the exam:
points: Identify topic, view and structure in the first read.
Detail questions: scan for keywords.
Inference: must follow logically, not just be possible.
Vocabulary: meaning in this sentence.
Avoid extreme and outside-knowledge options.
Daily editorial reading builds speed.

cards.title: Approach
cards.body: Find the **subject and main verb** first; most errors are agreement or tense errors. Then check prepositions, articles, pronouns and parallel structure. If nothing is wrong, choose 'No error' confidently.

cards.title: High-frequency rules
points: Neither/either … nor/or: verb agrees with the nearer subject
One of + plural noun + singular verb
Senior/junior/superior/prefer take 'to', not 'than'
Each/every + singular verb
Scarcely/hardly … when; no sooner … than

cards.title: Worked example
cards.body: 'Neither the manager nor his assistants **was** present.' The nearer subject 'assistants' is plural, so it should be '**were** present'.

cards.title: Read the whole sentence
cards.body: An error is often in a part that looks correct in isolation, e.g. a pronoun that does not match a noun two parts earlier. Read the full sentence once before judging any part.

cards.q: Find the error: 'Neither the manager nor his assistants (A) / was present (B) / at the meeting (C) / held yesterday (D).'
cards.explain: With 'neither … nor', the verb agrees with the nearer subject 'assistants', so 'was' should be 'were'.

cards.q: Find the error: 'One of my friend (A) / has joined (B) / SBI as (C) / a probationary officer (D).'
cards.explain: 'One of' takes a plural noun: 'One of my friends'.

cards.q: Find the error: 'He is senior (A) / than me (B) / in the bank (C) / No error (D).'
cards.explain: 'Senior' takes 'to': 'senior to me'.

notes.p: Error spotting and sentence improvement test **grammar rules**: subject–verb agreement, tenses, articles, prepositions, pronouns, comparisons and fixed structures. Read the whole sentence first; the error is often far from the word that causes it. If no rule is broken, choose 'No error'.
points: Find the **subject** and **main verb** first.
Check tense consistency across clauses.
Check every preposition and article.
Look for fixed pairs (no sooner … than, hardly … when).

notes.p: Most errors are here. Each example shows the error and the correction.
points: 'One of my friends **are** a banker' → **is** (the subject is 'one').
'Neither the manager nor the clerks **was** present' → **were** (verb agrees with the nearer subject 'clerks').
'The news **are** good' → **is** (news is singular).
'Each of the students **have** a book' → **has**.
'She is one of those women who **has** succeeded' → **have** ('who' refers to 'women').
'The team **is**' (as a unit) vs 'The team **are** arguing among themselves' (as individuals).

notes.p: These rules come up in almost every paper.
points: 'He has been working here **since** five years' → **for** five years (since + point of time, for + period).
'If I **was** you, I would apply' → **were** (unreal condition).
'If it **will** rain, we will stay home' → **rains** (no 'will' in the if-clause of a first conditional).
'No sooner did he reach **when** the train left' → **than**.
'Hardly had I sat down **than** the phone rang' → **when**.
