'**Unless** you do **not** work hard, you will fail' → 'Unless you work hard' (unless already means 'if not').
'Lest he **will** fall' → 'lest he **should** fall'.

notes.p:
Latin comparatives take 'to': **senior to, junior to, superior to, inferior to, prior to, prefer to**. So 'He is senior **than** me' → **senior to me**.

Avoid double comparatives: 'more better' → 'better'. Compare like with like: 'The salary of a PO is higher than **a clerk**' → '**that of** a clerk'.

Pronoun case: 'Between you and **I**' → 'between you and **me**' (object after a preposition). Use 'who' for subjects and 'whom' for objects.

**Sentence improvement method:** read the sentence with each option; reject options that break any rule above, then choose the one that is grammatical **and** keeps the original meaning.
These catch even good readers.
points: Being distracted by a long phrase between subject and verb.
Missing errors in the **last part** because you expected 'No error'.
Choosing a grammatical option that changes the meaning (in improvement questions).
Ignoring collective nouns and 'each/every'.
Over-correcting a sentence that is actually fine.

notes.p: Ten-second checklist.
points: Find subject → match verb.
Neither/nor, either/or: verb follows nearer subject.
Since = point of time; for = duration.
Unreal 'if' → were; no 'will' in the if-clause.
No sooner … than; hardly/scarcely … when.
Senior/junior/prior/prefer → to.
Unless already includes 'not'.

cards.title: What it tests
cards.body: A passage with blanks; you choose the word that fits **grammar, meaning and collocation**. Usually 5–10 questions in prelims. New formats include 'which word is correctly placed' and double fillers.

cards.title: Read the whole passage once
cards.body: Skim the passage before filling any blank to get its tone (positive/negative) and topic. Many blanks depend on the sentence **after** the blank, not before it.

cards.title: Elimination checklist
points: Grammar: part of speech, tense, singular/plural
Collocation: 'take a decision', 'bridge the gap', 'heavy rain'
Tone: positive word for a positive sentence
Connectors: however (contrast), therefore (result), moreover (addition)

cards.title: Worked example
cards.body: 'The RBI ___ the repo rate unchanged.' Options: kept, made, held up, put. 'Keep the rate unchanged' is the natural collocation → **kept**.

cards.q: 'The new scheme aims to ___ the gap between rural and urban banking.'
cards.explain: 'Bridge the gap' is the standard collocation.

cards.q: 'Credit growth was strong; ___, deposit growth lagged behind.'
cards.explain: The two clauses contrast, so 'however' fits.

notes.p: A cloze test is a short passage with blanks. You choose the word that fits **grammar, meaning and tone** together. Variants include **single fillers**, **double fillers** (two blanks in one sentence), **word-swap** and **phrase replacement**. Banks usually give 5–10 such questions.
points: Read the **whole passage once** before filling any blank.
Identify the **part of speech** needed (noun, verb, adjective, adverb).
Check **tense and number** to match the sentence.
Choose the word that fits the passage's overall tone.

notes.p: Many blanks are linking words. Decide the relationship between the two ideas first.
points: **Contrast:** however, although, despite, yet, whereas.
**Cause:** because, since, as, due to, owing to.
**Result:** therefore, hence, thus, consequently.
**Addition:** moreover, furthermore, besides, in addition.
**Grammar note:** 'despite' and 'in spite of' take a noun ('despite the rain'); 'although' takes a clause ('although it rained'). 'Despite **of**' is always wrong.

notes.p:
**Example 1:** "______ the rise in costs, the company managed to ______ its profits."
Options: (A) Because, lose (B) Despite, maintain (C) Although, cut (D) Since, double
Step 1: The ideas contrast (costs rose, but profits were held) → a contrast word.
Step 2: 'the rise in costs' is a noun phrase → 'despite' (not 'although', which needs a clause).
Step 3: 'managed to' signals success → 'maintain'.
Answer: **(B) Despite, maintain**.

**Example 2:** "The RBI kept the repo rate unchanged, ______ inflation remained above its comfort level."
Options: although / as / unless / despite.
The second clause gives the **reason** → **as**. 'Although' would wrongly suggest contrast; 'despite' cannot introduce a full clause.

Some words naturally go together (**collocations**): pay attention, commit a crime, heavy rain, bear in mind, meet a deadline, raise a loan, curb inflation, bridge a gap. If two options mean nearly the same, the natural collocation is usually correct.

Also use **context clues**: words like 'unlike', 'similarly', 'instead' or a definition in the next sentence often reveal the missing word.
Avoid these.
points: Choosing a word that fits the sentence but not the passage's tone.
Ignoring singular/plural agreement in the blank.
Picking 'although' before a noun phrase.
In double fillers, checking only the first blank.
Over-thinking rare words; the simpler word often fits best.

notes.p:
In **word-swap** questions, two highlighted words in a sentence or passage may be in each other's places. Read the sentence with the words exchanged; if both now fit grammar and meaning, they should be swapped.

In **phrase replacement**, a bold phrase may be wrong. Test each option in the sentence and check tense, number and idiom. 'No replacement required' is a valid answer when the original is already correct; do not change a correct sentence just because an option looks more formal.
Keep in mind:
points: Read the whole passage first.
Part of speech → tense/number → meaning → tone.
Despite + noun; although + clause.
Identify contrast, cause, result or addition for connectors.
Trust natural collocations.
In double fillers, both words must fit.

cards.title: Find the opener
cards.body: The opening sentence introduces the topic and can stand alone. It rarely starts with a **pronoun** (he, it, this, they) or a connector (however, therefore, also).

cards.title: Mandatory pairs
cards.body: Look for pairs that must sit together: a noun and the pronoun referring to it, a problem and its solution, 'first' and 'second', a general statement and its example. Two or three such pairs usually fix the whole order.

cards.title: Use the options
cards.body: Once you know the opener, eliminate options that start differently. Often only two options remain; check a single pair to choose between them.

cards.title: Closing sentence
cards.body: The last sentence usually **concludes**, sums up, or states the way forward ('Bridging this gap is the next challenge'). Connectors like 'thus' and 'therefore' are common at the end.

cards.q: Arrange: P – However, many of them still lack access to formal credit. Q – India has made rapid progress in opening bank accounts for the poor. R – Bridging this gap is the next big challenge for financial inclusion. S – Over 50 crore Jan Dhan accounts have been opened since 2014.
cards.explain: Q introduces the topic, S gives data, P contrasts ('However'), R concludes ('this gap').

cards.q: Which sentence is least likely to be the opener of a paragraph?
options: Digital lending has grown rapidly in India.
This has raised concerns about data privacy.
Banks are investing heavily in technology.
The RBI regulates all scheduled banks.
cards.explain: 'This' refers to something said earlier, so the sentence cannot open the paragraph.

notes.p: You are given 4–6 sentences in random order and must arrange them into a logical paragraph. Modern papers also ask for the **odd sentence out**, a **fixed sentence** position, or **connecting sentences**. The skill is spotting **links between sentences**.
points: Find the **opening** sentence.
Find **mandatory pairs** (sentences that must be together).
Use the options to eliminate quickly.
Find the **closing** sentence (conclusion, result, suggestion).

notes.h: How to find the opening and the links
notes.p:
An opening sentence introduces the topic and **stands alone**. It usually does not begin with a pronoun (he, it, this, they) or a connector (however, therefore, also).

Links that create mandatory pairs:
points: **Pronoun reference:** 'This growth' must follow the sentence that mentions growth.
**Articles:** 'a scheme' first, then 'the scheme'.
**Connectors:** 'However' follows the idea it contrasts; 'therefore' follows a reason.
**Time order:** 1991 before 2016; 'first' before 'later'.
**General → specific:** a broad statement before examples.
**Acronyms:** full form ('Unified Payments Interface (UPI)') before the short form.

notes.p:
Arrange:
A. However, many small traders still prefer cash because they fear hidden charges.
B. Digital payments have grown rapidly in India over the past decade.
C. This growth has been driven mainly by UPI, which allows instant transfers from a mobile phone.
D. Clear communication that most everyday UPI payments carry no charge for users could therefore speed up adoption.

Step 1 (opening): B introduces the topic and has no pronoun or connector → **B first**.
Step 2 (pair): 'This growth' in C refers to the growth in B → **B–C**.
Step 3: 'However' in A contrasts the growth with continued cash use → **C–A**.
Step 4: 'therefore' in D draws a conclusion from A's 'fear of hidden charges' → **A–D**.
Answer: **B C A D**.

In **odd sentence** questions, four sentences form a paragraph and one is about a related but different topic. Build the paragraph first; the sentence that has no link is the odd one.

In **fixed-position** questions ("sentence C is fixed as the third"), place C first and build around it; this removes many options immediately.

**Timing tip:** a para jumble should take about 60–75 seconds. If you have found the opener and one mandatory pair, check which options contain both; often only one does, and you can move on without fixing the full order.
These lead to wrong orders.
points: Choosing a sentence with a pronoun or connector as the opener.
Linking sentences by repeated words without checking meaning.
Ignoring time order clues (years, 'earlier', 'now').
Building the full order before checking options; options can confirm pairs quickly.
In odd-one-out, picking the sentence that is merely different in style.

notes.p: Remember:
points: Opener: independent, introduces topic.
Pronouns and 'the' point back to earlier sentences.
However/therefore follow the idea they react to.
Full form before abbreviation.
Use options to test mandatory pairs.
Closer: conclusion, result or suggestion.

chapters.title: Vocabulary: synonyms, antonyms, idioms & phrasal verbs

cards.title: How vocabulary is tested
cards.body: Bank English rarely asks isolated synonyms now. Vocabulary appears inside **RC (meaning in context)**, **cloze**, **fillers**, **word usage** and **idiom/phrase** questions. Learn words in sentences, not lists.

cards.title: Useful roots
points: bene = good (benefit, benevolent); mal = bad (malice, malfunction)
chron = time (chronic, chronology); ver = truth (verify, veracity)
am/phil = love (amiable, philanthropy); mis/miso = hate (misanthrope)
pre = before; post = after; re = again; sub = under; trans = across

cards.title: Frequent idioms
points: Bite the bullet — face a hard situation bravely
Cut corners — do something cheaply or carelessly
A blessing in disguise — a good thing that seemed bad
Keep at bay — prevent from coming near
Pull one’s weight — do one’s fair share
In the red — in debt / making losses

cards.title: Phrasal verbs
points: Call off — cancel; Carry out — perform
Bring about — cause; Put off — postpone
Look into — investigate; Turn down — reject
Make up for — compensate; Run out of — exhaust supply

cards.title: Context first
cards.body: For "meaning in context", replace the word with each option in the passage sentence. The right option keeps both meaning and tone; a dictionary meaning that does not fit the context is a trap.

cards.q: Synonym of "frugal":
cards.explain: Frugal = economical in spending.

cards.q: "To bite the bullet" means:
options: to face a difficult situation bravely
cards.explain: Idiom for accepting something unpleasant with courage.

cards.q: Antonym of "obscure":
cards.explain: Obscure = unclear; evident = clear.

notes.p: SBI and IBPS papers test vocabulary through context. A strong vocabulary speeds up reading comprehension, makes cloze tests easier and helps in the descriptive paper. The efficient way to build it is reading an editorial daily and noting 5–8 new words with the sentence in which they appeared.

Roots let you guess unfamiliar words. **Benevolent** (bene = good, vol = wish) means kind. **Chronic** (chron = time) means lasting a long time. **Malpractice** (mal = bad) is improper professional conduct.

**Worked example 1:** "The minister’s *equivocal* reply satisfied no one." Options: clear, ambiguous, angry, brief.
equi = equal, voc = voice → speaking in two ways → **ambiguous**. "Satisfied no one" supports a reply that avoided commitment.

**Worked example 2:** "Inflation has been *tenacious*, staying above target for months." Options: weak, persistent, sudden, mild. Context ("staying… for months") → **persistent**.

Idioms are fixed expressions whose meanings are not literal. Frequently tested: **at the eleventh hour** (at the last moment), **burn the midnight oil** (work late), **hit the nail on the head** (be exactly right), **a dark horse** (an unexpected winner), **turn a blind eye** (ignore deliberately), **a red-letter day** (memorable day), **the lion’s share** (largest part).

In "phrase replacement" questions, the error is often a wrong preposition in a fixed phrase: "comply **with**", "abide **by**", "consist **of**", "deal **with**".

**Worked example 3:** "Having missed the first two deadlines, the contractor finally delivered the project **at the eleventh hour**." Options: (a) at 11 o’clock (b) very early (c) at the last possible moment (d) after the deadline. The context of missed deadlines and "finally" points to **(c)**. Option (d) is a trap: the sentence says he delivered, implying it was just in time.

In idiom questions, the literal meaning is almost never the answer. Eliminate literal options first, then choose the one that fits the sentence’s situation.
Pairs often tested in word usage:
points: Affect (verb) / effect (noun; verb = bring about).
Principal (main; head) / principle (rule).
Complement (complete) / compliment (praise).
Stationary (not moving) / stationery (paper items).
Eminent (famous) / imminent (about to happen).
Economic (of the economy) / economical (thrifty).

notes.p:
Daily: read one editorial; note new words with their sentence; revise yesterday’s list. Weekly: 50-word self-test with sentences. Group words by theme (economy, environment, governance) because bank RCs draw from these themes. Use flashcards and say each word in a sentence aloud.

Keep a personal word bank in three columns: **word**, **meaning in your own words**, **sentence from the source**. Review it in spaced intervals — the next day, after three days, after a week — because recall drops quickly without revision. For antonyms, learn words in pairs (lavish–frugal, transparent–opaque, scarce–abundant, candid–evasive). Mock tests will show which themes keep recurring; give them extra time.
Vocabulary toolkit.
points: Learn words in context.
Use roots to guess meanings.
Substitute options into the sentence.
Know common idioms and phrasal verbs.
Watch confusable pairs.
Revise daily; test weekly.

cards.title: Single and double fillers
cards.body: Read the whole sentence, decide the **tone** (positive/negative) and **logic** (contrast, cause, addition), predict a word, then match options. In double fillers, eliminate options where either word fails.

cards.title: Grammar checks
cards.body: The blank must fit grammatically: part of speech, tense, singular/plural, and fixed prepositions (e.g. "averse **to**", "capable **of**").

cards.title: Word usage
cards.body: Questions show a word used in several sentences and ask which usages are correct, or give a word that fits all sentences. Check meaning and part of speech in each.

cards.title: Logic markers
points: Contrast: although, despite, however, but → opposite tone
Cause/result: because, since, so, hence → same direction
Addition: moreover, and, also → same tone
Definition clues: i.e., that is, which means

cards.title: Eliminate fast
cards.body: Remove options that break grammar first; then compare the remaining two on meaning. Most double fillers are solved by testing one blank thoroughly.

cards.q: "The new policy will ____ small businesses."
cards.explain: A verb meaning "influence" is needed: affect.

cards.q: "Despite the ____ rains, farmers ____ a good harvest."
cards.explain: "Despite" signals contrast: heavy rains yet a good harvest.

cards.q: "She bought new ____ for the office."
cards.explain: Stationery = paper and writing materials (uncountable).

notes.p:
Fillers test vocabulary, grammar and logic at once. Mains papers add twists: **double fillers**, **multiple blanks with a common word**, and **word usage** (which sentences use a word correctly). Each takes about 30–45 seconds with practice.

In Prelims, expect 3–5 filler or word-usage questions; in Mains they are often combined with phrase replacement or connector questions.

1. Read the full sentence before looking at options.
2. Identify the logic marker (despite, because, moreover).
3. Decide the tone of the blank (positive/negative).
4. Predict a word, then check options.
5. Confirm grammar: part of speech, number, tense, preposition.

**Worked example 1:** "The company’s profits were ____, so it ____ its expansion plans."
Options: (a) robust, accelerated (b) dismal, accelerated (c) robust, shelved (d) dismal, announced.
"So" signals result. Robust profits → accelerate expansion; dismal profits → shelve plans. Only (a) is consistent → **(a)**.

**Worked example 3:** "The economist’s forecast proved ____; growth was far weaker than she had predicted."
Options: prescient, accurate, optimistic, cautious.
The second clause says reality was weaker than predicted, so the forecast was too positive → **optimistic**. "Prescient" and "accurate" contradict the clue; "cautious" points the wrong way.

**Worked example 4:** "Neither the manager nor the clerks ____ aware of the change." With "neither…nor", the verb agrees with the nearer subject (clerks) → **were**.

**Worked example 2:** Which sentences use "bear" correctly?
I. I cannot bear the noise.
II. The documents bear his signature.
III. Please bear the shop open till nine.
I (tolerate) ✓, II (carry/display) ✓, III ✗ (should be "keep"). Answer: **I and II**.

For a "word that fits all blanks" question, the common word usually has several meanings (e.g. "issue": a problem, to release, an edition).

**Worked example 4:** Find one word that fits both: "The bank will ____ new bonds next month." / "Climate change is a pressing ____ for farmers." → **issue** (verb: release; noun: problem). Words such as *issue*, *bear*, *charge*, *check*, *yield* and *interest* are favourites because each has several meanings, including a banking one (interest on a loan, yield on a bond, a charge on assets).
Common grammar checks:
points: Collocations: "make a decision", "take a step", "pay attention".
Prepositions: "prefer X to Y", "different from", "similar to".
Articles: "an hour", "a university" (sound, not spelling).
Verb forms after "despite" and "in spite of": noun or -ing.
Subjunctive: "It is essential that he be present."

notes.p: Avoid these.
points: Choosing a word that fits only the first blank.
Ignoring "despite/although" contrast.
Picking a sophisticated word that does not collocate.
Overlooking singular/plural agreement with the blank.

notes.p: Fillers in short.
points: Read the whole sentence first.
Find the logic marker.
Predict, then match.
Grammar filter: part of speech, number, preposition.
Double fillers: both words must fit.
Word usage: check meaning in each sentence.

cards.title: Connectors show logic
cards.body: A connector links two ideas and shows their relation: **contrast**, **cause**, **result**, **addition**, **condition**, **time** or **example**.

cards.title: Connector groups
points: Contrast: although, though, however, whereas, despite, nevertheless
Cause: because, since, as, owing to, due to
Result: therefore, hence, thus, consequently, so
Condition: if, unless, provided that, in case
Addition: moreover, furthermore, besides, in addition

cards.title: Sentence starters
cards.body: Mains questions give two sentences and a starter ("Despite…", "Not only…", "Had…"). Choose the starter that combines them without changing meaning or grammar.

cards.title: Structures to remember
points: Despite / In spite of + noun or -ing
Although + clause (subject + verb)
Not only … but also (inversion when it starts the sentence)
Had + subject + past participle = If + subject + had …
No sooner … than; Hardly … when

cards.title: Meaning test
cards.body: After combining, ask: does the new sentence say exactly what the two originals said? A connector that changes the relation (cause into contrast) is wrong even if grammatical.

cards.q: "He was ill. He attended the meeting." Best combination begins with:
cards.explain: Contrast: although he was ill, he attended.

cards.q: "Unless you work hard, you will not pass" means:
options: If you do not work hard, you will not pass
If you work hard, you will not pass
You will pass without hard work
Work hard only if you want to fail
cards.explain: Unless = if not.

cards.q: "Despite" must be followed by:
options: a full clause with subject and verb
cards.explain: Despite the rain / despite being tired.

notes.p:
Connectors decide the logic of a paragraph. They are tested directly (fill in the connector), indirectly (para jumbles, cloze) and in **sentence combining** with starters or column matching. A clear grasp of the seven relations — contrast, cause, result, addition, condition, time, example — solves most of these questions.

Connectors also signal the structure of passages. "However" announces a turn in the argument; "for instance" introduces support; "in short" or "thus" marks a conclusion. Spotting them speeds up RC (where the author’s main point usually follows a contrast word) and para jumbles (where a sentence starting with "however" or "this" cannot open the paragraph).

**Worked example 1:** "The bank cut its lending rate. Loan demand did not rise."
Starter options: (a) Despite (b) Because (c) Since (d) As.
The relation is contrast → "**Despite** the bank cutting its lending rate, loan demand did not rise." (a) ✓.

**Worked example 2:** "The RBI had raised the repo rate. Then inflation started easing." Starter: "**No sooner** had…" → "No sooner had the RBI raised the repo rate than inflation started easing." Note the pair **no sooner … than** and the inversion "had the RBI".

**Worked example 4:** "She completed the course. She found a job." Starter: "Having…" → "**Having completed** the course, she found a job." The participle phrase must refer to the subject of the main clause; "Having completed the course, a job was found" is wrong because the job did not complete the course (a dangling modifier).
When negative or limiting adverbs open a sentence, the auxiliary comes before the subject:
points: Not only did the bank cut rates, but it also eased norms.
Hardly had the meeting begun when the power failed.
Seldom do we see such growth.
Had I known, I would have helped (= If I had known…).
Should you need help, call us (= If you should need…).

notes.p:
Mains also gives Column I (sentence beginnings) and Column II (endings). Match by grammar first (singular/plural, tense, connector), then by meaning. Typically only 2–3 combinations are correct; answer options list combinations such as "A-E, C-D".

**Worked example 3:** Column I: "Although the demand was high," — Column II: (D) "the supply remained limited." / (E) "therefore prices fell." Contrast with "although" → **D**; E uses "therefore", which clashes with "although".
Avoid these.
points: Using "although … but" together (only one is needed).
"Despite of" — wrong; use "despite" or "in spite of".
"No sooner … when" — wrong; it is "no sooner … than".
Forgetting inversion after negative openers.

notes.p: Connector rules.
points: Identify the relation first.
Despite + noun/-ing; although + clause.
No sooner … than; hardly … when.
Negative opener → inversion.
Unless = if not.
Meaning must not change after combining.

cards.title: RBI at a glance
cards.body: Set up on **1 April 1935** under the RBI Act, 1934 (Hilton Young Commission), nationalised on **1 January 1949**. HQ moved from Kolkata to **Mumbai** in 1937. It issues currency, regulates banks, manages forex and acts as banker to the government and to banks.

cards.title: Monetary Policy Committee
cards.body: The **6-member MPC** (3 from RBI incl. the Governor, 3 appointed by the government) sets the repo rate; the Governor has a casting vote. Target: **CPI inflation 4% ± 2%**, retained by the government for **April 2026 – March 2031** (notified March 2026).

cards.title: Policy rates (corridor)
points: Repo: rate at which RBI lends to banks against G-secs
SDF (Standing Deposit Facility) = repo − 0.25%: floor of the corridor, no collateral needed
MSF (Marginal Standing Facility) = repo + 0.25%: ceiling; banks can dip into SLR
Bank Rate = MSF rate
Fixed-rate reverse repo (3.35%) exists but SDF has replaced it as the floor since April 2022

cards.title: Reserve ratios
points: CRR: % of NDTL kept as cash with RBI; earns no interest
SLR: % of NDTL kept by the bank itself in cash, gold or approved securities
NDTL = net demand & time liabilities
OMO: RBI buys/sells G-secs to add/absorb liquidity

cards.title: Rates as of August 2026
cards.body: As of the **August 2026 MPC review**: repo **5.25%**, SDF **5.00%**, MSF and Bank Rate **5.50%**, stance **neutral**; CRR **3%** (cut from 4% in tranches to Nov 2025), SLR **18%**. Rates change every two months, so check rbi.org.in before your exam.

cards.title: Direction logic
cards.body: To fight inflation RBI **raises** repo/CRR (tightening). To support growth it **cuts** them (easing). Cutting CRR releases lendable funds directly; cutting repo lowers the cost of borrowing.

cards.q: Which facility forms the floor of the RBI's liquidity adjustment facility corridor today?
cards.explain: Since April 2022 the SDF (repo − 25 bps) is the floor; MSF is the ceiling.

cards.q: If the repo rate is 5.25%, the MSF rate is:
cards.explain: MSF = repo + 25 basis points = 5.50%.

cards.q: CRR is maintained as a percentage of:
cards.explain: Both CRR and SLR are calculated on NDTL.

notes.p:
The **Reserve Bank of India** was set up on **1 April 1935** under the **RBI Act, 1934**, on the recommendation of the **Hilton Young Commission**. It was privately owned at first and **nationalised on 1 January 1949**. Its central office moved from Kolkata to **Mumbai in 1937**. The RBI is headed by a Governor appointed by the Central Government.

The RBI wears many hats, and questions often ask which function a statement describes.
points: **Monetary authority:** controls money supply and interest rates to keep prices stable.
**Issuer of currency:** issues all notes except the ₹1 note (issued by the Government of India).
**Regulator and supervisor** of banks and many NBFCs (Banking Regulation Act, 1949).
**Banker to the government** and **banker's bank** (lender of last resort).
**Manager of foreign exchange** under FEMA, 1999.
**Regulator of payment systems** under the Payment and Settlement Systems Act, 2007.

notes.h: Monetary Policy Committee and inflation targeting
notes.p:
Since a 2016 amendment to the RBI Act, India follows **flexible inflation targeting**. The Government, in consultation with the RBI, sets the target for **CPI (Consumer Price Index) inflation**; it has been **4% with a band of ±2%** (2–6%).

The **Monetary Policy Committee (MPC)** has **6 members**: 3 from the RBI (Governor, a Deputy Governor and one officer) and 3 external members appointed by the Government. Decisions are by majority, and the **Governor has a casting vote** in a tie. The Act requires at least four meetings a year; in practice the MPC meets about every two months.

If inflation stays **outside the band for three consecutive quarters**, the RBI must send a report to the Government explaining why and what it will do.

notes.h: Quantitative tools: how each one works
notes.p: These tools change the **quantity and cost of money** in the economy. Exact values change at MPC meetings, so **check the latest RBI announcement** for current figures; learn the **logic** here.
points: **Repo rate:** the rate at which RBI lends overnight to banks against government securities. The main policy rate.
**Standing Deposit Facility (SDF):** banks park surplus funds with RBI **without collateral**; it is the **floor** of the interest-rate corridor (set below repo).
**Marginal Standing Facility (MSF):** emergency overnight borrowing, allowed by dipping into SLR securities; the **ceiling** of the corridor (set above repo). **Bank Rate** is aligned with MSF.
**CRR:** a share of a bank's **NDTL** kept as cash with RBI; earns no interest.
**SLR:** a share of NDTL kept by the bank in cash, gold or approved securities.
**Open Market Operations (OMO):** RBI buys government securities to inject liquidity, sells to absorb it.

notes.h: Worked example: how CRR and SLR limit lending
notes.p:
Suppose a bank has **NDTL of ₹1,000 crore**, and assume (for practice only) CRR = 4% and SLR = 18%.
Step 1: CRR = 4% of 1,000 = **₹40 crore** kept with RBI as cash.
Step 2: SLR = 18% of 1,000 = **₹180 crore** kept in approved securities.
Step 3: Funds left for lending ≈ 1,000 − 40 − 180 = **₹780 crore**.
If CRR is cut by 1 percentage point to 3%, CRR becomes ₹30 crore and **₹10 crore** more can be lent. That is why a CRR cut directly increases lendable funds, while a repo cut works by making borrowing cheaper.

**Direction logic:** to fight high inflation, RBI **raises** repo/CRR or sells securities (tightening). To support growth, it **cuts** them or buys securities (easing).

**Qualitative (selective) tools** target specific sectors rather than total money supply: **margin requirements** on loans against goods or shares, **moral suasion** (persuading banks), **selective credit controls** and **direct action** against non-compliant banks.

**Transmission** is how quickly policy-rate changes reach borrowers. Since **1 October 2019**, banks must link new floating-rate retail and MSME loans to an **external benchmark** (such as the repo rate), so changes now pass through faster than under the older MCLR and base-rate systems.
These distinctions are asked often.
points: CRR is kept **with RBI**; SLR is kept **by the bank itself**.
SDF (floor) needs **no collateral**; MSF (ceiling) lets banks use SLR securities.
The ₹1 note is issued by the **Government**, not RBI.
The inflation target uses **CPI**, not WPI.

notes.p: One-liners to remember.
points: RBI: 1 April 1935; nationalised 1 January 1949; HQ Mumbai.
MPC: 6 members, Governor has casting vote.
Target: CPI 4% ± 2%.
Corridor: SDF (floor) < repo < MSF = Bank Rate (ceiling).
CRR cut → more lendable funds immediately.
Current rates: check the latest RBI announcement.

cards.title: Scheduled vs non-scheduled
cards.body: A **scheduled bank** is listed in the **Second Schedule of the RBI Act, 1934** and can borrow from RBI. Scheduled commercial banks include public sector, private, foreign, regional rural, small finance and payments banks. Cooperative banks form a separate tier.

cards.title: Nationalisation timeline
points: 1955: Imperial Bank of India → State Bank of India
19 July 1969: 14 banks (deposits > ₹50 crore)
15 April 1980: 6 banks (deposits > ₹200 crore)
2019–20: mega-mergers leave 12 public sector banks

cards.title: Regional Rural Banks
cards.body: Set up from **2 October 1975** (Narasimham Working Group), governed by the **RRB Act, 1976**. Shareholding: **Centre 50%, sponsor bank 35%, state 15%**. Under 'One State, One RRB' consolidation (effective 1 May 2025) the number fell to **28 RRBs**.

cards.title: Differentiated banks
cards.body: **Payments banks** accept deposits up to **₹2 lakh** per customer and offer remittances, but **cannot lend** or issue credit cards. **Small finance banks** must give 75% of credit to priority sectors and serve small borrowers.

cards.title: Easy recall
cards.body: Remember 14 (1969) + 6 (1980) = 20 nationalised banks. The 1969 threshold was ₹50 crore and 1980 was ₹200 crore: 50 → 200.

cards.q: How many banks were nationalised on 19 July 1969?
cards.explain: 14 major banks with deposits above ₹50 crore were nationalised in 1969; 6 more followed in 1980.

cards.q: Shareholding of an RRB (Centre : sponsor bank : state) is:
cards.explain: Under the RRB Act, the Centre holds 50%, the sponsor bank 35% and the state government 15%.

cards.q: Which of these can a payments bank NOT do?
cards.explain: Payments banks are barred from lending and from issuing credit cards.

notes.h: Structure of the Indian banking system
notes.p:
At the top is the **RBI**. Banks are classed as **scheduled** (listed in the **Second Schedule of the RBI Act, 1934**) or **non-scheduled**. Scheduled banks can borrow from RBI and must meet its reserve rules.

**Scheduled commercial banks** include public sector banks, private sector banks, foreign banks, regional rural banks, small finance banks and payments banks. **Cooperative banks** form a separate tier, owned by members.
points: **Public sector banks (PSBs):** Government holds the majority stake (e.g. SBI, PNB, Bank of Baroda).
**Private banks:** majority private ownership (e.g. HDFC Bank, ICICI Bank).
**Foreign banks:** branches or wholly owned subsidiaries of overseas banks.
**RRBs:** rural focus, jointly owned by Centre, sponsor bank and state.
**Small finance banks and payments banks:** 'differentiated' banks with limited roles.

notes.p: Cooperative banks are registered under state or multi-state cooperative laws and are regulated by RBI for banking functions under the **Banking Regulation Act, 1949**. A **2020 amendment** strengthened RBI's powers over them after failures in some urban cooperative banks.
points: **Urban Cooperative Banks (UCBs):** serve towns and cities.
**Short-term rural credit (three tiers):** State Cooperative Bank → District Central Cooperative Bank → **Primary Agricultural Credit Society (PACS)** at village level.
**Long-term rural credit:** State and Primary Cooperative Agriculture and Rural Development Banks.
**NABARD** supervises rural cooperative banks (StCBs and DCCBs) and RRBs.

notes.p: The three **Presidency Banks** (Bank of Bengal 1806, Bank of Bombay 1840, Bank of Madras 1843) merged in **1921** to form the **Imperial Bank of India**, which became the **State Bank of India on 1 July 1955**.
points: **19 July 1969:** 14 banks with deposits above ₹50 crore nationalised.
**15 April 1980:** 6 more banks with deposits above ₹200 crore nationalised.
**1969:** Lead Bank Scheme assigns districts to banks for coordinated development.
**1991 and 1998:** Narasimham Committees recommend banking-sector reforms.
**2017:** SBI absorbs its five associate banks and Bharatiya Mahila Bank.
**2019–2020:** mergers (e.g. Vijaya and Dena into Bank of Baroda; OBC and United Bank into PNB) leave **12 PSBs**.

notes.h: Regional Rural Banks and differentiated banks
notes.p:
**RRBs** were set up from **2 October 1975** (based on the Narasimham Working Group) and are governed by the **RRB Act, 1976**. Shareholding is **Centre 50% : sponsor bank 35% : state 15%**. After several rounds of mergers, 'One State, One RRB' consolidation took effect on **1 May 2025**, leaving 28 RRBs.

**Payments banks** can accept deposits (with a per-customer limit, currently ₹2 lakh; check RBI for changes), offer remittances and debit cards, but **cannot lend or issue credit cards**. **Small finance banks** take deposits and lend, with a strong focus on small borrowers: **75% of their credit must go to priority sectors**.

**Question:** A bank was nationalised in 1980. What was its deposit size threshold and how many banks were nationalised with it?
Step 1: 1980 is the second round.
Step 2: Threshold = deposits above **₹200 crore**; number = **6 banks**.
Step 3: Total nationalised in both rounds = 14 + 6 = **20**.
Memory hook: '14 at 50, 6 at 200'.
Frequently confused points.
points: SBI was formed in **1955**, not nationalised in 1969.
RRB shares are 50 : 35 : 15 (Centre : sponsor : state), not 50 : 15 : 35.
Payments banks **cannot lend**; small finance banks can.
Scheduled = listed in the **Second** Schedule of the RBI Act.
NABARD, not RBI directly, supervises RRBs and rural cooperative banks.

notes.p: Memorise these.
points: Imperial Bank (1921) → SBI (1 July 1955).
12 PSBs after the 2020 mergers.
Payments banks: deposits yes, loans no.
SFBs: 75% priority-sector lending.
PACS → DCCB → StCB is the short-term cooperative chain.

chapters.title: Payment systems: UPI, NEFT, RTGS, IMPS

cards.title: Who runs what
cards.body: **RBI** owns and runs **NEFT and RTGS**. **NPCI** (set up in 2008 by RBI and the Indian Banks' Association) runs **UPI, IMPS, RuPay, NACH, AePS, NETC FASTag and Bharat BillPay**. The legal base is the **Payment and Settlement Systems Act, 2007**.

cards.title: Quick comparison
points: NEFT: batches every half hour, 24×7 since 16 Dec 2019, no minimum
RTGS: real-time gross settlement, minimum ₹2 lakh, 24×7 since 14 Dec 2020
IMPS: instant 24×7, up to ₹5 lakh per transaction
UPI: instant, on IMPS rails, launched 2016; mostly ₹1 lakh per P2P transaction

cards.title: UPI family
cards.body: **BHIM** (NPCI app), **UPI Lite** (small payments without PIN), **UPI 123PAY** (feature phones), **UPI AutoPay** (recurring mandates), **RuPay credit card on UPI**, and UPI links with other countries (e.g. Singapore PayNow). Limits change often; check npci.org.in.

cards.title: Gross vs net
cards.body: RTGS = **gross** (each transaction settled individually, in real time). NEFT = **deferred net** settlement in batches. This difference is a favourite one-mark question.

cards.q: The minimum amount for an RTGS transfer is:
cards.explain: RTGS is meant for large-value transfers with a minimum of ₹2 lakh; there is no upper limit.

cards.q: UPI is operated by:
cards.explain: The National Payments Corporation of India runs UPI.

cards.q: NEFT settles transactions on a:
options: Deferred net basis in half-hourly batches
cards.explain: NEFT uses deferred net settlement in batches every half hour, 24×7.

notes.p: Payment systems are regulated by the RBI under the **Payment and Settlement Systems Act, 2007**. The RBI directly runs **NEFT** and **RTGS**. The **National Payments Corporation of India (NPCI)**, set up in **2008** by the RBI and the Indian Banks' Association as a not-for-profit company, runs retail systems.
points: **NPCI products:** UPI, IMPS, RuPay, NACH, AePS, NETC FASTag, Bharat BillPay (BBPS), BHIM app, CTS operations.
**RBI-run:** NEFT, RTGS.
**Complaints:** RBI's Integrated Ombudsman Scheme (2021) covers banks, NBFCs and payment system participants.

notes.h: NEFT, RTGS, IMPS and UPI compared
notes.p: The main difference is **how and when money is settled**.
points: **RTGS (Real Time Gross Settlement):** each transaction settled **individually and instantly**; meant for large values (minimum ₹2 lakh); available 24×7 since December 2020.
**NEFT (National Electronic Funds Transfer):** **deferred net settlement** in half-hourly batches; no minimum amount; 24×7 since December 2019.
**IMPS (Immediate Payment Service):** instant, 24×7, works by mobile number + MMID or account + IFSC.
**UPI (Unified Payments Interface):** launched in **2016**; instant transfers using a **virtual payment address (UPI ID)** or QR code; built on IMPS rails.
Per-transaction limits for IMPS and UPI are revised from time to time; **check NPCI/RBI announcements** for current values.

notes.p:
Codes appear as easy one-mark questions.

**IFSC (Indian Financial System Code)** has **11 characters**: the first **4 letters** identify the bank, the **5th is always 0** (reserved), and the **last 6** identify the branch. Example: in 'SBIN0001234', SBIN = State Bank of India, 0 = reserved, 001234 = branch.

**MICR** code is **9 digits** printed on cheques: city (3) + bank (3) + branch (3). The **Cheque Truncation System (CTS)** clears cheques using images, so the physical cheque need not travel.
These appear in GA and interview questions.
points: **NACH:** bulk and recurring payments (salaries, subsidies, EMIs) and mandates.
**AePS:** cash withdrawal and balance enquiry using **Aadhaar and fingerprint** at a business correspondent.
**BBPS (Bharat BillPay):** one platform for utility and other bill payments.
**NETC FASTag:** electronic toll collection using RFID tags.
**e-RUPI:** a prepaid, purpose-specific digital voucher (launched 2021).
**e₹ (CBDC):** RBI's digital rupee, piloted from late 2022 in wholesale and retail versions.
**UPI variants:** UPI Lite (small PIN-less payments), UPI 123PAY (feature phones), UPI AutoPay (recurring).

notes.h: Worked example: choosing the right system
notes.p:
A business must send **₹15 lakh** to a supplier **at 11 pm on a Sunday**, with immediate final settlement.
Step 1: Amount is above ₹2 lakh → RTGS is allowed.
Step 2: Time is late night on a holiday → RTGS and NEFT both run **24×7** now.
Step 3: Requirement is **individual, real-time final settlement** → **RTGS**.
NEFT would also work but settles in batches (net), so it is not 'real-time gross'.
Watch these.
points: RTGS is **gross**; NEFT is **net** (batch) settlement.
NEFT and RTGS are run by **RBI**, not NPCI.
NPCI was set up in **2008**; UPI launched in **2016**.
IFSC is 11 characters with a zero as the 5th character.
Quoting old UPI/IMPS limits; check the latest circular.

notes.p: Key facts.
points: PSS Act 2007; NPCI 2008; UPI 2016.
RTGS: real-time gross, min ₹2 lakh, 24×7 (Dec 2020).
NEFT: half-hourly batches, no minimum, 24×7 (Dec 2019).
IFSC 11 characters; MICR 9 digits.
AePS uses Aadhaar + biometrics.
e₹ = RBI's CBDC.
Limits change: check NPCI/RBI before the exam.

cards.title: PM Jan Dhan Yojana (2014)
cards.body: Announced on 15 August 2014, launched 28 August 2014. **Zero-balance** BSBD account, **RuPay** debit card with **₹2 lakh** accident cover (accounts after 28.8.2018), and an overdraft of up to **₹10,000**. Over 50 crore accounts; a majority held by women.

cards.title: Jan Suraksha schemes (2015)
points: PMSBY: accident cover ₹2 lakh, premium ₹20/year, age 18–70
PMJJBY: life cover ₹2 lakh, premium ₹436/year, age 18–50
APY: pension ₹1,000–5,000/month at 60, join at 18–40

cards.title: PM Mudra Yojana (2015)
points: Shishu: up to ₹50,000
Kishor: ₹50,000 – ₹5 lakh
Tarun: ₹5 – 10 lakh
Tarun Plus: ₹10 – 20 lakh (for those who repaid Tarun loans)

cards.title: Other schemes
cards.body: **Stand-Up India** (2016): loans of ₹10 lakh – ₹1 crore to SC/ST and women entrepreneurs. **PM SVANidhi** (2020): working-capital loans for street vendors. RBI's **Financial Inclusion Index** (FI-Index) measures progress on a 0–100 scale each year.

cards.title: Remember the numbers
cards.body: 20 and 436 are the premiums; 2 lakh is the cover for both PMSBY and PMJJBY. APY age 18–40 and PMJJBY age 18–50 are the most common confusions.

cards.q: The annual premium of PMSBY is:
cards.explain: PMSBY premium was revised from ₹12 to ₹20 per year in 2022; PMJJBY is ₹436.

cards.q: Under PM Mudra Yojana, 'Shishu' loans go up to:
cards.explain: Shishu covers loans up to ₹50,000.

cards.q: The entry age for Atal Pension Yojana is:
cards.explain: APY is open to people aged 18–40, with pension starting at 60.

notes.p:
**Financial inclusion** is making basic financial services (a bank account, credit, insurance, pension and payments) **available and affordable** to everyone, especially the poor, women and rural people. India's approach rests on the **JAM trinity** (Jan Dhan accounts, Aadhaar identity and Mobile phones), which made **Direct Benefit Transfer (DBT)** of subsidies possible.

RBI's **Financial Inclusion Index (FI-Index)**, published annually since 2021, measures progress on a **0–100** scale using three dimensions: **Access, Usage and Quality**, with usage given the highest weight.
Announced on 15 August 2014 and launched on **28 August 2014**, PMJDY aims at one basic bank account for every unbanked adult.
points: **Zero-balance** Basic Savings Bank Deposit (BSBD) account.
**RuPay debit card** with accident insurance cover of **₹2 lakh** (for accounts opened after 28 August 2018; ₹1 lakh earlier).
**Overdraft** facility up to **₹10,000** for eligible account holders.
Over 50 crore accounts, a majority held by women; the scheme channels DBT payments.

notes.p: Three schemes launched in May 2015 provide low-cost insurance and pension through bank accounts.
points: **PMSBY** (Suraksha Bima): accident death/disability cover **₹2 lakh**; premium **₹20 per year**; age **18–70**.
**PMJJBY** (Jeevan Jyoti Bima): life cover **₹2 lakh** for death due to any cause; premium **₹436 per year**; enrol at age **18–50**.
**Atal Pension Yojana (APY):** guaranteed pension of **₹1,000–5,000 per month** from age 60; join between **18 and 40**; administered by **PFRDA**.
Premiums are auto-debited from the bank account; renewal is yearly (June to May cover period).

notes.p:
**PM MUDRA Yojana (2015)** offers collateral-free loans to non-farm micro enterprises through banks, NBFCs and MFIs; refinance is provided by **MUDRA Ltd**, a SIDBI subsidiary.

**Worked example:** A tailor needs **₹3,50,000** to buy machines. Which Mudra category?
Shishu covers up to ₹50,000; Kishor covers ₹50,000 to ₹5 lakh; Tarun covers ₹5 to 10 lakh.
₹3.5 lakh lies between ₹50,000 and ₹5 lakh → **Kishor**.
points: **Shishu:** up to ₹50,000. **Kishor:** ₹50,000–5 lakh. **Tarun:** ₹5–10 lakh. **Tarun Plus:** ₹10–20 lakh (for good repayers of Tarun loans).
**Stand-Up India (2016):** ₹10 lakh–₹1 crore for greenfield enterprises; each bank branch to support at least one **SC/ST** and one **woman** borrower.
**PM SVANidhi (2020):** working-capital loans for street vendors.
**SHG–Bank Linkage (NABARD, 1992)** and **business correspondents** take banking to villages.

notes.p: Often confused.
points: PMSBY premium ₹20 (accident) vs PMJJBY ₹436 (life).
PMJJBY entry age 18–50; APY entry age 18–40; PMSBY 18–70.
APY is run by PFRDA, not LIC.
PMJDY launched 28 August 2014 (announced 15 August).
Scheme amounts are revised in budgets; check the latest figures before the exam.

notes.p: Lock these in.
points: JAM = Jan Dhan + Aadhaar + Mobile → DBT.
PMJDY: zero balance, RuPay, ₹2 lakh accident cover, ₹10,000 OD.
PMSBY ₹20, PMJJBY ₹436, both ₹2 lakh cover.
APY ₹1,000–5,000 pension, join 18–40.
Mudra: Shishu ≤ ₹50k, Kishor ≤ ₹5 lakh, Tarun ≤ ₹10 lakh, Tarun Plus ≤ ₹20 lakh.
Stand-Up India: ₹10 lakh–₹1 crore, SC/ST and women.
FI-Index: Access, Usage, Quality; 0–100.

cards.title: Basel norms
cards.body: Issued by the **Basel Committee on Banking Supervision** (hosted by the BIS in Basel, Switzerland). **Basel III** (after the 2008 crisis) rests on three pillars: **minimum capital**, **supervisory review** and **market discipline**. It also added leverage and liquidity ratios (LCR, NSFR).

cards.title: Capital numbers in India
points: CRAR (capital to risk-weighted assets) minimum: 9% (Basel III global: 8%)
Capital conservation buffer: 2.5%
So effective minimum = 11.5%
LCR: high-quality liquid assets ≥ 100% of 30-day net outflows

cards.title: Non-performing assets
cards.body: A loan becomes an **NPA** when interest or principal is overdue for **more than 90 days**. Classes: **substandard** (NPA ≤ 12 months), **doubtful** (substandard for 12 months), and **loss** (identified as uncollectable).

cards.title: Recovery laws
cards.body: **SARFAESI Act, 2002**: banks can seize and sell secured assets **without court** after a **60-day** notice (not for loans under ₹1 lakh). **DRTs** (RDDBFI Act, 1993) for claims of ₹20 lakh and more. **IBC, 2016**: time-bound insolvency resolution (180 days, extendable).

cards.title: Related terms
cards.body: **PCA** (Prompt Corrective Action): RBI restrictions on weak banks. **ARC**: asset reconstruction company that buys bad loans. **Provision Coverage Ratio**: provisions ÷ gross NPA. **Gross NPA** includes provisions; **net NPA** = gross NPA − provisions.

cards.q: A loan is classified as NPA when dues remain overdue for more than:
cards.explain: The 90-day overdue norm has applied since 2004.

cards.q: Under SARFAESI, how many days' notice must a bank give before taking possession of security?
cards.explain: Section 13(2) of the SARFAESI Act requires a 60-day demand notice.

cards.q: Effective minimum capital requirement (CRAR + conservation buffer) for Indian banks under Basel III is:
cards.explain: RBI's 9% CRAR plus the 2.5% capital conservation buffer = 11.5%.

notes.p: A bank lends depositors' money. If loans go bad, the bank's own **capital** must absorb the losses so depositors are protected. The **Basel Committee on Banking Supervision**, based at the **Bank for International Settlements (BIS) in Basel, Switzerland**, sets global standards for how much capital banks must hold.
points: **Basel I (1988):** focused on **credit risk**; minimum capital of 8% of risk-weighted assets.
**Basel II (2004):** added operational and market risk and introduced **three pillars**: minimum capital, supervisory review, market discipline.
**Basel III (2010, after the 2008 crisis):** keeps the three pillars and adds higher-quality capital, buffers, a **leverage ratio** and liquidity ratios (**LCR** and **NSFR**).

notes.h: Basel III numbers in India and a worked CRAR example
notes.p:
**CRAR (Capital to Risk-weighted Assets Ratio)** = total capital ÷ risk-weighted assets × 100. India's minimum is **9%** (stricter than the global 8%), plus a **capital conservation buffer of 2.5%**, giving an effective **11.5%**. Within this, Common Equity Tier 1 must be at least 5.5%. Large systemically important banks (D-SIBs, such as SBI, HDFC Bank and ICICI Bank) must hold extra capital.

**Worked example:** A bank has capital of **₹1,150 crore** and risk-weighted assets of **₹10,000 crore**.
CRAR = 1,150 ÷ 10,000 × 100 = **11.5%** → it just meets the effective minimum.
If RWA grows to ₹12,000 crore with the same capital: 1,150 ÷ 12,000 × 100 ≈ **9.6%** → below 11.5%, so the bank must raise capital or slow lending.

A loan becomes an **NPA** when interest or principal remains **overdue for more than 90 days**. Before that, banks track early stress as **Special Mention Accounts**: **SMA-0** (1–30 days overdue), **SMA-1** (31–60), **SMA-2** (61–90). For crop loans the test is two crop seasons (short-duration crops) or one season (long-duration crops).
points: **Substandard:** NPA for up to 12 months.
**Doubtful:** remained substandard for 12 months.
**Loss:** identified as uncollectable but not yet written off.
**Net NPA = Gross NPA − provisions.**
**Provision Coverage Ratio (PCR) = provisions ÷ gross NPA × 100.**

notes.p:
A bank has gross advances of ₹10,000 crore, gross NPAs of **₹500 crore** and provisions of **₹350 crore**.
Gross NPA ratio = 500 ÷ 10,000 × 100 = **5%**.
Net NPA = 500 − 350 = **₹150 crore**.
PCR = 350 ÷ 500 × 100 = **70%**.
Net NPA ratio (approx.) = 150 ÷ (10,000 − 350) × 100 ≈ **1.55%** (net advances exclude provisions).
A higher PCR means the bank is better cushioned against loan losses.
Banks have several legal routes to recover bad loans.
points: **SARFAESI Act, 2002:** secured creditors can take possession of and sell the security **without going to court**, after a **60-day** notice; not used for loans below ₹1 lakh.
**Debt Recovery Tribunals** (RDDBFI Act, 1993) handle claims of **₹20 lakh and above**.
**Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code (IBC), 2016:** time-bound resolution (180 days, extendable by 90) via the NCLT.
**Asset Reconstruction Companies (ARCs)** buy bad loans from banks; **NARCL** (2021) is the government-backed 'bad bank' for large stressed loans.
**Prompt Corrective Action (PCA):** RBI restrictions on banks breaching capital, asset-quality or leverage thresholds.

notes.p: Often confused facts.
points: Three pillars were introduced in **Basel II**, retained in Basel III.
India's CRAR minimum is 9%, not 8%.
NPA after **more than 90 days**, not 90 days exactly.
Doubtful = substandard for 12 months (not NPA for 12 months).
SARFAESI notice is **60 days**; DRT threshold is **₹20 lakh**.

notes.p: Key numbers.
points: Basel Committee at BIS, Basel.
LCR ≥ 100% of 30-day net outflows.
Net NPA = gross − provisions; PCR = provisions ÷ gross NPA.
SARFAESI 2002 (60-day notice), DRT ₹20 lakh+, IBC 2016 (180 + 90 days).

chapters.title: Financial markets: money, capital, bond & forex

cards.title: Two halves
cards.body: The **money market** deals in funds for up to one year (liquidity). The **capital market** deals in long-term funds — shares and bonds — through **primary** (new issues) and **secondary** (trading) markets.

cards.title: Money market instruments
points: Call money: overnight; notice money: 2–14 days; term money: 15 days–1 year
Treasury bills: 91, 182, 364 days, issued at a discount by RBI for the Centre
Commercial paper (CP): unsecured, by companies; 7 days–1 year
Certificate of deposit (CD): by banks, 7 days–1 year
Repo / TREPS: collateralised borrowing

cards.title: Capital market
cards.body: **Primary**: IPO, FPO, rights issue, private placement, QIP. **Secondary**: stock exchanges such as **BSE** (est. 1875, Asia’s oldest) and **NSE**. Benchmark indices: **Sensex** (30 stocks) and **Nifty 50**.

cards.title: Regulators
cards.body: **RBI** regulates money, government securities and forex markets. **SEBI** (set up 1988, statutory since 1992) regulates securities markets, mutual funds and intermediaries. **IRDAI** regulates insurance; **PFRDA** pensions.

cards.title: Bonds and special instruments
cards.body: **G-secs** (Centre), **SDLs** (states), corporate bonds, **masala bonds** (rupee-denominated, issued abroad), **green bonds**, and **sovereign gold bonds**. Bond prices move **opposite** to interest rates.

cards.title: Remember by tenure
cards.body: Sort every instrument by maximum tenure and issuer. Many questions simply ask "who issues X" or "what is the tenure of Y".

cards.q: The longest standard tenure of a Treasury bill in India is:
cards.explain: T-bills are 91, 182 and 364 days.

cards.q: SEBI got statutory powers in:
cards.explain: Set up in 1988; statutory under the SEBI Act, 1992.

cards.q: Masala bonds are:
cards.explain: The currency risk lies with the foreign investor.

notes.p: Financial markets move savings to borrowers. For bank exams, know each segment, its instruments, who issues them, their tenure, and who regulates them. In RBI Grade B and NABARD, this extends to the functioning of markets and recent reforms; in PO/Clerk, factual one-liners dominate.

The money market handles short-term funds (up to one year) and is regulated by the **RBI**.

**Call/notice/term money:** inter-bank unsecured lending — overnight (call), 2–14 days (notice), 15 days to 1 year (term).
**Treasury bills:** short-term borrowing of the Central Government, issued at a **discount** and redeemed at face value.
**Commercial paper:** unsecured promissory note of highly rated companies.
**Certificate of deposit:** negotiable time deposit issued by banks.
**Repo and TREPS:** borrowing against securities; the RBI’s policy repo rate anchors these rates.

**Worked example 1:** A 91-day T-bill with face value ₹100 is bought at ₹98.50. The gain of ₹1.50 over 91 days gives an annualised yield of about (1.50/98.50) × (365/91) ≈ **6.1%**.

**Primary market:** companies raise fresh capital through IPOs, follow-on offers, rights issues, qualified institutional placements and private placements.
**Secondary market:** existing securities trade on exchanges; India moved to **T+1** settlement for equities in 2023.

Key institutions: **depositories** (NSDL, CDSL) hold securities in electronic form; **clearing corporations** guarantee settlement; **mutual funds** pool savings and report a daily **NAV**.

Bond prices and yields move in opposite directions. If a bond pays a fixed ₹8 a year on face value ₹100 and market rates rise to 10%, new buyers will pay less than ₹100 so that ₹8 gives them a higher yield.

**Worked example 2:** A perpetual bond pays ₹8 a year. At a market yield of 8% its price is 8/0.08 = ₹100; at 10% it is 8/0.10 = **₹80**. A rise in rates cut the price by 20%.

This is why rising policy rates cause **mark-to-market losses** on banks’ bond portfolios.

The **foreign exchange market** is regulated by the RBI under **FEMA, 1999**. India follows a **managed float**: the rupee’s value is market-determined, with RBI intervention to curb excess volatility. **Derivatives** — forwards, futures, options and swaps — derive value from an underlying asset and are used for hedging and speculation.
points: Current account convertibility since 1994; capital account partially convertible.
Futures are standardised and exchange-traded; forwards are customised and over-the-counter.

notes.p: Mix-ups to avoid.
points: CP is issued by companies; CD by banks.
T-bills pay no coupon — they are issued at a discount.
SEBI was set up in 1988 but became statutory in 1992.
Bond prices fall when yields rise.

notes.p: Facts to recall.
points: Money market ≤ 1 year (RBI); capital market > 1 year (SEBI).
T-bills: 91/182/364 days.
CP: companies; CD: banks.
BSE 1875; Sensex 30; Nifty 50.
Masala bonds: rupee bonds issued abroad.
Bond price ↓ when yield ↑.

cards.title: Regulators
cards.body: **RBI** — banks, NBFCs, payments, money and forex markets. **SEBI** — securities. **IRDAI** — insurance. **PFRDA** — pensions (NPS, APY). **IBBI** — insolvency professionals and processes under the IBC, 2016.

cards.title: Development finance institutions
points: NABARD (1982) — agriculture and rural development
SIDBI (1990) — MSME finance
EXIM Bank (1982) — export–import finance
NHB (1988) — housing finance
NaBFID (2021) — infrastructure financing

cards.title: Market infrastructure
cards.body: **NPCI** (2008) runs UPI, IMPS, RuPay, NACH and FASTag. **CCIL** clears government securities and forex trades. **Credit information companies** such as CIBIL maintain credit histories.

cards.title: DICGC
cards.body: The **Deposit Insurance and Credit Guarantee Corporation**, a wholly owned RBI subsidiary, insures bank deposits up to **₹5 lakh per depositor per bank** (principal and interest), raised from ₹1 lakh in 2020.

cards.title: Learn by pairing
cards.body: Make a two-column list: institution → year, HQ and role. NABARD, SIDBI, EXIM, NHB and NPCI are the most asked.

cards.q: DICGC insures deposits up to:
cards.explain: ₹5 lakh per depositor per bank since 2020.

cards.q: NABARD was established in:
cards.explain: Set up on 12 July 1982 on the recommendation of the CRAFICARD committee.

cards.q: Which body regulates the National Pension System?
cards.explain: PFRDA regulates NPS and Atal Pension Yojana.

notes.p:
India’s financial system has sector-specific regulators. The **Reserve Bank of India** (established 1 April 1935, nationalised 1949) regulates banks, NBFCs, payment systems, and the money, government securities and foreign exchange markets. **SEBI** regulates securities markets. **IRDAI** regulates insurers. **PFRDA** regulates pension funds. The **Financial Stability and Development Council (FSDC)**, chaired by the Finance Minister, coordinates among them.

Self-regulatory and industry bodies also appear in questions: the **Indian Banks’ Association (IBA)** represents banks; the **Association of Mutual Funds in India (AMFI)** represents mutual funds; **FEDAI** sets conduct rules for the forex market. They are not statutory regulators, a distinction examiners like to test.

DFIs provide long-term or sector-specific finance:

**NABARD** (1982) — apex development bank for agriculture and rural areas; refinances cooperative banks and RRBs; manages funds such as the Rural Infrastructure Development Fund.
**SIDBI** (1990) — principal institution for MSME promotion and finance.
**EXIM Bank** (1982) — finances and promotes India’s international trade.
**NHB** (1988) — refinances housing finance; regulation of housing finance companies moved to the RBI in 2019.
**NaBFID** (2021) — a DFI for infrastructure.

**Worked recall example:** "Which institution would refinance an RRB’s crop loans?" → **NABARD**. "Which would support a small manufacturer’s machinery loan through refinance?" → **SIDBI**.

The **National Payments Corporation of India (NPCI)**, an umbrella organisation promoted by the RBI and the Indian Banks’ Association, operates retail payment systems: **UPI, IMPS, RuPay, NACH, AePS, BBPS** and **NETC FASTag**. The **Clearing Corporation of India (CCIL)** clears government securities, money market and forex transactions. **Depositories** NSDL and CDSL hold securities electronically.

**DICGC** insures each depositor’s balances in a bank up to ₹5 lakh, covering savings, current, fixed and recurring deposits. Deposits of governments and inter-bank deposits are excluded.

**Worked example:** A depositor has ₹3 lakh in a savings account and ₹4 lakh in an FD at the same failed bank. Insured amount = **₹5 lakh** (the limit is per depositor per bank, not per account). If the FD were at a different bank, both banks’ balances would be insured separately.

The **Insolvency and Bankruptcy Board of India (IBBI)** oversees processes under the IBC, 2016; the **NCLT** adjudicates corporate insolvency cases.
Mix-ups to avoid.
points: NHB now under the Government, but HFC regulation moved to RBI (2019).
NPCI is not a regulator; RBI regulates payment systems under the PSS Act, 2007.
DICGC limit is per depositor per bank, not per account.
SEBI regulates mutual funds; IRDAI regulates ULIPs’ insurers.

notes.p: Institution list.
points: RBI 1935; SEBI statutory 1992; IRDAI (1999 Act); PFRDA (2013 Act).
NABARD 1982; EXIM 1982; NHB 1988; SIDBI 1990; NaBFID 2021.
NPCI 2008 — UPI, RuPay, IMPS, FASTag.
DICGC cover ₹5 lakh per depositor per bank.
IBBI and NCLT under the IBC, 2016.
FSDC chaired by the Finance Minister.

chapters.title: Government schemes for the economy & welfare

cards.title: How to learn schemes
cards.body: For each scheme note: **launch year, ministry, target group, benefit, and implementing agency**. Figures change through budget announcements, so revise from the latest official source before the exam.

cards.title: Credit and enterprise
points: PM MUDRA Yojana (2015): Shishu (≤ ₹50,000), Kishore (₹50,000–₹5 lakh), Tarun (₹5–10 lakh); Tarun Plus up to ₹20 lakh added in 2024
Stand-Up India (2016): ₹10 lakh–₹1 crore for SC/ST and women entrepreneurs
PM SVANidhi (2020): working-capital loans for street vendors
PM Vishwakarma (2023): support for traditional artisans

cards.title: Farmers and rural
points: PM-KISAN (2019): ₹6,000 a year in three instalments
PM Fasal Bima Yojana (2016): crop insurance with low farmer premium
Kisan Credit Card: short-term crop credit
PMAY-Gramin: rural housing; MGNREGA (2005 Act): 100 days of wage work

cards.title: Health, savings and social security
points: Ayushman Bharat PM-JAY (2018): health cover up to ₹5 lakh per family per year
Sukanya Samriddhi Yojana (2015): savings for the girl child
Atal Pension Yojana (2015): pension for the unorganised sector, entry age 18–40
PMJDY, PMJJBY, PMSBY: see the financial inclusion chapter

cards.title: Group by beneficiary
cards.body: Revise schemes in groups — farmers, MSMEs, women, students, unorganised workers. Questions often name the beneficiary and ask for the scheme.

cards.q: Annual income support under PM-KISAN is:
cards.explain: ₹6,000 a year in three equal instalments.

cards.q: Under MUDRA, the "Kishore" category covers loans of:
cards.explain: Shishu ≤ ₹50,000; Kishore to ₹5 lakh; Tarun to ₹10 lakh.

cards.q: Stand-Up India provides loans in the range of:
cards.explain: For SC/ST and women entrepreneurs setting up greenfield enterprises.

notes.p:
Government schemes are among the most frequently tested topics in bank General/Financial Awareness, and they reappear in interviews. The financial inclusion chapter covers PMJDY and the three social-security schemes; this chapter covers credit, farm, housing, health and savings schemes.

Always verify current figures (premiums, limits, interest rates) from **PIB**, the ministry website or the latest Budget speech, because they are revised.

A good way to store schemes is a one-line card: **name — year — ministry — beneficiary — benefit**. Example: "PM SVANidhi — 2020 — Housing & Urban Affairs — street vendors — collateral-free working-capital loans with interest subsidy." Revisit the cards after each Budget and update any changed limits.

**PM MUDRA Yojana** (2015) provides collateral-free loans to non-corporate, non-farm micro enterprises through banks, NBFCs and MFIs. Categories: **Shishu** (up to ₹50,000), **Kishore** (₹50,000–₹5 lakh), **Tarun** (₹5–10 lakh); the Union Budget 2024–25 added **Tarun Plus** (₹10–20 lakh) for borrowers who repaid Tarun loans.

**Stand-Up India** (2016) — bank loans between ₹10 lakh and ₹1 crore to at least one SC/ST borrower and one woman borrower per bank branch for greenfield enterprises.

**PM SVANidhi** (2020) — small working-capital loans for street vendors, with interest subsidy and digital incentives.

**Credit Guarantee Fund Trust for Micro and Small Enterprises (CGTMSE)** guarantees collateral-free MSE loans.

**PM-KISAN** (2019) transfers ₹6,000 a year to eligible farmer families in three instalments through DBT.
**PM Fasal Bima Yojana** (2016) insures crops; farmers pay a small share of the premium (2% for kharif, 1.5% for rabi food and oilseed crops, 5% for commercial/horticultural crops).
**Kisan Credit Card** — revolving short-term credit for crops, extended to animal husbandry and fisheries.
**MGNREGA** — legal guarantee of 100 days of wage employment a year to rural households.
**PMAY-G** — pucca houses for rural households; **DAY-NRLM** — SHG-based livelihoods.

**Ayushman Bharat PM-JAY** (2018) — secondary and tertiary hospital cover of up to ₹5 lakh per family per year; the cover was extended to all citizens aged 70 and above in 2024.
**PMAY-Urban** — housing for the urban poor.
**Sukanya Samriddhi Yojana** (2015) — small-savings account for a girl child under 10.
**Atal Pension Yojana** (2015) — guaranteed pension of ₹1,000–₹5,000 a month from age 60, administered by PFRDA.

**Worked recall example:** A 25-year-old woman wants to start a ₹40 lakh manufacturing unit. Matching scheme? **Stand-Up India** (₹10 lakh–₹1 crore, women eligible, greenfield).
Mix-ups to avoid.
points: MUDRA is not a direct lender to borrowers; it refinances lenders.
PM-KISAN is income support, not insurance.
APY entry age is 18–40; PMJJBY and PMSBY are insurance, not pensions.
Scheme figures change — use the latest notification.

notes.p: Scheme sheet.
points: MUDRA: Shishu/Kishore/Tarun/Tarun Plus.
Stand-Up India: ₹10 lakh–₹1 crore (SC/ST, women).
PM-KISAN: ₹6,000/year, three instalments.
PMFBY: 2% kharif, 1.5% rabi, 5% commercial.
PM-JAY: ₹5 lakh per family per year.
APY: pension ₹1,000–5,000; entry 18–40.

chapters.title: Union Budget, fiscal terms & Economic Survey

cards.title: Constitutional basis
cards.body: The Budget is the **Annual Financial Statement (Article 112)**. Money is withdrawn through the **Appropriation Bill (Art. 114)**; tax proposals pass in the **Finance Bill** (a money bill, Art. 110). Since 2017 the Budget is presented on **1 February** and includes the Railway Budget.

cards.title: Deficits
points: Fiscal deficit = total expenditure − (revenue receipts + non-debt capital receipts)
Revenue deficit = revenue expenditure − revenue receipts
Primary deficit = fiscal deficit − interest payments
Effective revenue deficit = revenue deficit − grants for creation of capital assets

cards.title: Receipts and expenditure
cards.body: **Revenue receipts**: taxes and non-tax revenue (dividends, fees). **Capital receipts**: borrowings, loan recoveries, disinvestment. **Capital expenditure** creates assets or reduces liabilities; **revenue expenditure** does not.

cards.title: Economic Survey
cards.body: Prepared by the **Economic Division of the Department of Economic Affairs** under the **Chief Economic Adviser**, tabled before the Budget. It reviews the economy’s performance and outlook.

cards.title: Deficit example
cards.body:
Revenue receipts 100; non-debt capital receipts 5; total expenditure 150 (revenue 120); interest 30.
FD = 150 − 105 = **45**; RD = 120 − 100 = **20**; PD = 45 − 30 = **15**.

cards.q: Fiscal deficit minus interest payments equals:
cards.explain: Primary deficit removes past-debt interest.

cards.q: The Annual Financial Statement is mentioned in Article:
cards.explain: Art. 112; Art. 280 is the Finance Commission.

cards.q: The Economic Survey is prepared under the guidance of the:
cards.explain: Economic Division of DEA, Ministry of Finance, under the CEA.

notes.p:
The **Union Budget** is the government’s statement of estimated receipts and expenditure for the coming financial year (April–March). It has three parts: the Annual Financial Statement, the demands for grants, and the Finance Bill. Parliament discusses it in general, then department-wise; members can move **cut motions**. Before the full Budget passes, a **vote on account** may allow spending for part of the year.

Since 2017 the Budget is presented on 1 February so that funds are available from 1 April, and the separate Railway Budget was merged into it.

**Revenue receipts** do not create liabilities or reduce assets: tax revenue (income tax, corporation tax, GST, customs, excise) and non-tax revenue (dividends from PSUs and RBI, interest, fees).
**Capital receipts** create liabilities or reduce assets: market borrowings, small-savings funds, loan recoveries and disinvestment.

**Capital expenditure** builds assets (roads, railways) or gives loans; it lifts long-term growth. **Revenue expenditure** pays for running the government: salaries, interest, subsidies.

**Worked example 1:** Revenue receipts ₹30 lakh crore; recoveries and disinvestment ₹1 lakh crore; total expenditure ₹48 lakh crore, of which revenue expenditure ₹37 lakh crore; interest payments ₹11 lakh crore.
Fiscal deficit = 48 − (30 + 1) = **₹17 lakh crore**.
Revenue deficit = 37 − 30 = **₹7 lakh crore**.
Primary deficit = 17 − 11 = **₹6 lakh crore**.

**Worked example 2:** If GDP is ₹340 lakh crore, the fiscal deficit of ₹17 lakh crore is 17/340 = **5% of GDP**.

Fiscal deficit shows the government’s total borrowing need; primary deficit shows how much of it is for current, not past, obligations.

The **FRBM Act, 2003** set targets for reducing deficits and debt; it has been amended several times, and the Centre now presents a debt-focused path in recent Budgets. The **Finance Commission** (Art. 280) recommends how taxes are shared between the Centre and states; the 15th Finance Commission recommended 41% devolution to states. The 16th Finance Commission covers 2026–31; check its accepted recommendations in the latest Budget. The **GST Council** (Art. 279A) sets GST rates; GST began on 1 July 2017.

The Survey is prepared by the Economic Division of the Department of Economic Affairs under the **Chief Economic Adviser** and tabled before the Budget. It reviews growth, inflation, fiscal position, external sector, and sectoral trends, and often introduces policy ideas. For exams, note its growth projection, key themes and new terminology — but verify numbers from the official document.
Mix-ups to avoid.
points: Borrowings are capital receipts, not revenue receipts.
Primary deficit = fiscal deficit − interest (not − capital expenditure).
Art. 112 (Budget) vs Art. 110 (money bill) vs Art. 280 (Finance Commission).
Economic Survey is not a constitutional requirement.

notes.p: Budget sheet.
points: Budget date: 1 February; Railway Budget merged 2017.
FD = expenditure − (revenue + non-debt capital receipts).
RD = revenue expenditure − revenue receipts.
PD = FD − interest.
FRBM Act 2003; GST from 1 July 2017.
Survey: Economic Division, DEA, under the CEA.

cards.title: Bretton Woods twins
points: IMF (1944 conference; HQ Washington, D.C.) — balance-of-payments support, surveillance, SDRs
World Bank Group (HQ Washington, D.C.) — IBRD, IDA, IFC, MIGA, ICSID
IMF reports: World Economic Outlook, Global Financial Stability Report
World Bank: World Development Report

cards.title: Development banks
points: ADB — 1966, Manila
AIIB — began 2016, Beijing
New Development Bank (BRICS) — Shanghai
BIS — 1930, Basel (hosts the Basel Committee)

cards.title: Trade and others
points: WTO — 1995, Geneva (successor to GATT)
FATF — 1989, Paris (anti-money laundering)
OECD — Paris; UNCTAD — Geneva (World Investment Report)
UNDP — Human Development Report; ILO — Geneva; FAO, IFAD, WFP — Rome

cards.title: Groupings
cards.body: **G20** (1999; India held the presidency in 2023), **BRICS** (expanded from 2024), **SCO**, **SAARC** (secretariat Kathmandu), **ASEAN** (secretariat Jakarta), **BIMSTEC** (secretariat Dhaka).

cards.title: Learn in a table
cards.body: Columns: organisation — founded — HQ — head (check current) — flagship report. Heads change; verify before the exam.

cards.q: Headquarters of the Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank:
cards.explain: AIIB is in Beijing; NDB is in Shanghai; ADB in Manila.

cards.q: The Human Development Report is published by:
cards.explain: UNDP publishes the HDR and the HDI.

cards.q: The Basel Committee on Banking Supervision is hosted by:
cards.explain: BIS in Basel hosts the BCBS.

notes.p:
International organisations appear in every bank GA paper — usually as headquarters, founding year, head, reports or India’s role. Names of heads and member lists change, so treat them as current affairs and confirm them before the exam. Founding facts and reports are stable.

India-specific facts are favourites: India is a founding member of the IMF, World Bank and WTO; it is a founding member of the AIIB and the NDB; it is a member of the BIS and the FATF (since 2010). Learn these together with each organisation’s main function.

Both were conceived at the **Bretton Woods Conference (1944)** and are headquartered in **Washington, D.C.**

The **IMF** promotes monetary cooperation and exchange-rate stability, lends to countries facing balance-of-payments problems, conducts surveillance (Article IV consultations), and issues **Special Drawing Rights (SDRs)**, valued against a basket of five currencies (US dollar, euro, Chinese renminbi, Japanese yen, pound sterling).

The **World Bank Group** has five institutions: **IBRD** (loans to middle-income countries), **IDA** (concessional loans and grants to the poorest), **IFC** (private-sector investment), **MIGA** (political-risk guarantees) and **ICSID** (investment disputes).

India’s **quota** in the IMF determines its voting share and borrowing access; quotas are reviewed periodically.

**Asian Development Bank** (1966, Manila) — Japan and the US are the largest shareholders; India is a major borrower.
**AIIB** (operations from 2016, Beijing) — China is the largest shareholder, India the second largest.
**New Development Bank** (Shanghai) — set up by BRICS countries.
**Bank for International Settlements** (1930, Basel) — the "central bank of central banks"; hosts the **Basel Committee**, which sets Basel norms.

**Worked recall example:** "Which organisation sets global anti-money-laundering standards and runs a grey list?" → **FATF** (Paris).

The **WTO** (1995, Geneva) replaced GATT and administers trade agreements; its highest body is the Ministerial Conference. UN specialised agencies: **ILO** (Geneva), **WHO** (Geneva), **UNESCO** (Paris), **FAO**, **IFAD** and **WFP** (all Rome), **UNEP** (Nairobi). **UNCTAD** publishes the World Investment Report; **UNDP** the Human Development Report.

**Worked recall example:** "India’s G20 presidency was in which year, and what was its theme?" → **2023**, "Vasudhaiva Kutumbakam — One Earth, One Family, One Future". The New Delhi summit admitted the **African Union** as a permanent member of the G20.
points: World Economic Forum (Geneva/Cologny): Global Gender Gap Report.
OECD (Paris): economic outlooks for member and partner countries.

notes.p: Mix-ups to avoid.
points: AIIB (Beijing) vs NDB (Shanghai) vs ADB (Manila).
World Development Report (World Bank) vs World Economic Outlook (IMF).
BIS is in Basel, not Geneva.
IFC lends to private firms, IDA to the poorest governments.

notes.p: HQ and report list.
points: IMF, World Bank — Washington, D.C.
ADB Manila; AIIB Beijing; NDB Shanghai; BIS Basel.
WTO, ILO, WHO, UNCTAD — Geneva; FAO, IFAD, WFP — Rome.
FATF, OECD, UNESCO — Paris.
HDR — UNDP; WDR — World Bank; WEO — IMF.
Heads change: verify before the exam.

chapters.title: Current affairs & static GK: a method

cards.title: What to cover
cards.body: Bank GA papers draw from the last **4–6 months** of current affairs (more for RBI/NABARD), weighted towards banking, economy, government schemes, appointments, reports and indices, summits, awards and sports.

cards.title: Primary sources
cards.body: Use **PIB** for government decisions, **RBI press releases** and the monetary policy statement for banking, **SEBI/IRDAI** circulars for markets, and one reliable newspaper. Monthly compilations help revision but check facts against primary sources.

cards.title: Static GK to keep ready
points: Bank HQs and taglines; RBI governors and deputy governors (verify)
Countries — capitals — currencies
Important days (e.g. 1 April: RBI foundation day)
National parks, dams, dances by state
Committees on banking reforms (Narasimham, Nachiket Mor, etc.)

cards.title: Note format
cards.body: One line per item: **what — who — where — when — number**. Tag each line by category (banking, economy, sports…). Short, tagged notes are easy to revise.

cards.title: Spaced revision
cards.body: Revise each week’s notes after 1 day, 1 week and 1 month. Before the exam, go through all tagged banking/economy items twice; they are the highest-yield categories.

cards.q: Which source is most authoritative for a new central government scheme announcement?
cards.explain: PIB carries official releases from ministries.

cards.q: The currency of Japan is:
cards.explain: Yuan (China), Won (Korea), Ringgit (Malaysia).

cards.q: For banking awareness, the best way to track changes in the repo rate is:
options: RBI’s monetary policy statement and press release
cards.explain: The RBI announces policy rates officially after MPC meetings.

notes.p:
Candidates often lose GA marks not from lack of reading but from poor retention. A **fixed method** — limited sources, short notes, spaced revision — beats reading many capsules once. GA is also the fastest section: 35–40 questions in about 15–20 minutes in Mains, so recall must be instant.

Weightage varies: in PO and Clerk Mains, banking and economy items usually form the largest block, followed by government schemes and miscellaneous current events. Plan your time to match.

Pick one daily source (a national newspaper’s economy and national pages) and one monthly compilation. Verify any fact you note against a primary source: **PIB** (government), **RBI** (banking, monetary policy, regulations), **SEBI** (markets), **ministry websites** (schemes). Avoid collecting PDFs you will not revise.
