For banking and economy, read the **RBI’s monetary policy statement**, the **Governor’s statement** and the "Statement on Developmental and Regulatory Policies" after every MPC meeting; they usually produce several questions. For schemes, the **Budget speech** and **PIB backgrounders** are reliable starting points.

Write one line per fact with five elements: what happened, who, where, when, and the key number.

**Worked example 1:** A news item about a policy-rate change becomes: "MPC — repo rate changed to X% (date); SDF/MSF adjusted; stance: …" — filled from the RBI press release, not memory.

**Worked example 2:** An appointment item: "Name — post — organisation — since (month/year)". Add the predecessor if it is a high-profile post. Tag both lines [Banking].

Static GK supports current affairs. Priorities for bank exams: headquarters and taglines of banks and insurers; financial institutions and their founding years; capitals and currencies; important days; state-wise national parks, festivals and dances; constitutional articles relevant to finance (110, 112, 280, 279A); and banking committees.

**Worked recall example:** A news item about a summit in a foreign city should trigger three links in your notes — the country’s capital, its currency and India’s relations with it. Linking static facts to current events improves recall and covers both question types at once.
points: Learn countries in the news with their capital and currency together.
Revise committees with the year and subject.

notes.p:
A practical cycle: daily 30–45 minutes reading and noting; weekly 60 minutes revising the week; monthly half-day revision plus a GA mock. In the final fortnight, revise only your notes and the last six months’ banking/economy items.

**Worked example 3:** With 90 days to Mains, you can do 12 weekly cycles and 3 monthly ones. If each weekly cycle covers about 60 one-line facts, you will have revised about 720 facts at least three times by exam day.
Method in brief.
points: 4–6 months for PO/Clerk; more for RBI/NABARD.
Primary sources: PIB, RBI, SEBI, ministries.
One-line tagged notes.
Spaced revision: day, week, month.
Static GK tied to current news.
Verify changing facts before the exam.

chapters.title: Banking products, terms & the NI Act

cards.title: Deposits
cards.body: **CASA** = current + savings deposits (low-cost funds). **Term deposits**: fixed (FD) and recurring (RD). Banks prefer a high CASA ratio because it lowers their cost of funds.

cards.title: Loans and advances
cards.body: **Term loan** — repaid in instalments; **cash credit** — drawing limit against stock/receivables; **overdraft** — drawing beyond balance; **bill discounting**. Secured loans are backed by collateral; unsecured ones are not.

cards.title: Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881
points: Negotiable instruments: promissory note, bill of exchange, cheque
Cheque validity: 3 months from its date
Section 138: dishonour of cheque for insufficient funds is an offence
Crossing (two parallel lines) → payable only through a bank account

cards.title: Key terms
points: Priority sector lending: 40% of ANBC (or CEOBE, whichever is higher) for domestic banks
EBLR: external benchmark (e.g. repo) for floating retail and MSE loans since Oct 2019
KYC under the PMLA, 2002 framework
Bancassurance: banks selling insurance products

cards.title: Know the parties
cards.body: Cheque: drawer (writes it), drawee (bank), payee (receives). Bill of exchange: drawer, drawee (who must pay), payee. Questions often swap these.

cards.q: A cheque is valid for:
cards.explain: RBI reduced validity to 3 months in 2012.

cards.q: Dishonour of a cheque for insufficient funds is dealt with under Section ___ of the NI Act:
cards.explain: Section 138 makes it a criminal offence.

cards.q: The overall priority sector lending target for domestic scheduled commercial banks is:
cards.explain: 40% of ANBC or CEOBE, whichever is higher.

notes.p: Banking terms appear in every bank GA paper, in descriptive answers and in interviews. Officers use them daily, so interview boards test them even when the written exam does not.

notes.h: Deposits and the cost of funds
notes.p:
**Current accounts** (businesses, no interest), **savings accounts** (individuals, modest interest), **fixed deposits** (lump sum for a term) and **recurring deposits** (monthly instalments). **CASA ratio** = (current + savings deposits) ÷ total deposits.

**Worked example 1:** A bank has current deposits ₹20,000 crore, savings ₹50,000 crore and term deposits ₹1,30,000 crore. CASA ratio = 70,000 ÷ 2,00,000 = **35%**. A higher CASA ratio usually means a lower cost of funds and better margins.

**Term loans** finance fixed assets and are repaid in EMIs. **Working-capital** limits — cash credit and overdraft — fund day-to-day operations; interest is charged only on the amount used. **Bill discounting** advances money against trade bills. **Non-fund-based** facilities (bank guarantees, letters of credit) do not involve an immediate outflow.

**Worked example 2:** A trader with a ₹10 lakh cash-credit limit uses ₹6 lakh for 30 days at 12% a year. Interest ≈ 6,00,000 × 12% × 30/365 ≈ **₹5,918** — only the used amount is charged.

**Retail loans** include home, vehicle, education and personal loans; **gold loans** are secured by jewellery with a loan-to-value cap set by the RBI. **EMI** = P × r × (1 + r)ⁿ ÷ [(1 + r)ⁿ − 1], where r is the monthly rate and n the number of months.

Under the **NI Act, 1881**, the three negotiable instruments are the **promissory note** (a promise to pay), the **bill of exchange** (an order to pay) and the **cheque** (a bill drawn on a bank, payable on demand). A cheque is valid for **three months**. **Section 138** makes dishonour for insufficient funds an offence, subject to notice requirements.

Crossing: **general** (two parallel lines) → pay only through a bank account; **account payee** → credit only to the payee’s account; **special** → name of a bank written between the lines. **CTS** (Cheque Truncation System) clears cheques through images.

**Priority sector lending (PSL):** agriculture, MSMEs, export credit, education, housing, social infrastructure, renewable energy and others; domestic banks must lend **40%** of ANBC/CEOBE, with sub-targets. **EBLR:** since 1 October 2019, new floating-rate loans to individuals and MSEs are linked to an external benchmark such as the repo rate. **KYC** and anti-money-laundering rules flow from the **PMLA, 2002** and RBI directions.
points: MCLR still applies to many older and corporate loans.
PSL shortfalls are deposited in funds such as RIDF.

notes.p: A computer takes **input**, **processes** it, **stores** it and gives **output**. The **CPU** has the **ALU** (arithmetic and logic), the **Control Unit** (directs operations) and **registers** (tiny, fastest storage).

**2nd:** transistors.
**3rd:** integrated circuits (ICs).
**4th:** microprocessors (personal computers).
**5th:** artificial intelligence, parallel processing.
By size/power: supercomputer > mainframe > minicomputer > microcomputer.

notes.p:
Memory is arranged from fastest and smallest to slowest and largest: **registers → cache → RAM → secondary storage (SSD/HDD)**.

**RAM** is **volatile** (loses data when power is off). **SRAM** (static) is faster and used for **cache**; **DRAM** (dynamic) is used for main memory. **ROM** is **non-volatile** and stores firmware such as the BIOS. Types: PROM (programmed once), EPROM (erased by UV light), EEPROM (erased electrically; flash memory is a type of EEPROM).
points: 1 byte = 8 bits; 1 nibble = 4 bits.
1 KB = 1,024 bytes; KB → MB → GB → TB → PB, each × 1,024.
Secondary storage: HDD (magnetic), SSD (flash), optical discs (CD/DVD/Blu-ray).

notes.p:
Binary = base 2, octal = base 8, decimal = base 10, hexadecimal = base 16 (A–F = 10–15). One octal digit = 3 bits; one hex digit = 4 bits.

**Worked example 1: decimal 45 to binary.** Divide by 2 and record remainders:
45 ÷ 2 = 22 r **1**; 22 ÷ 2 = 11 r **0**; 11 ÷ 2 = 5 r **1**; 5 ÷ 2 = 2 r **1**; 2 ÷ 2 = 1 r **0**; 1 ÷ 2 = 0 r **1**.
Read remainders bottom to top: **101101**.
Check: 32 + 8 + 4 + 1 = 45 ✓.

**Worked example 2: binary 110110 to hex and octal.**
Hex: group 4 bits from the right → 0011 | 0110 → 3 | 6 → **36₁₆**.
Octal: group 3 bits → 110 | 110 → 6 | 6 → **66₈**.
Check in decimal: 110110₂ = 32 + 16 + 4 + 2 = 54; 3 × 16 + 6 = 54 ✓; 6 × 8 + 6 = 54 ✓.

**Worked example 3:** hex 2F = 2 × 16 + 15 = **47**.
**System software** (operating system, device drivers, utilities) manages the hardware; **application software** (word processors, browsers, banking apps) serves the user.

**Compiler:** translates the whole program at once (C, C++).
**Interpreter:** translates and runs line by line (Python, classic BASIC).
**Assembler:** converts assembly language to machine code.
**Universal logic gates:** NAND and NOR (any circuit can be built from them).

cards.title: Networks
cards.body: **LAN** (building), **MAN** (city), **WAN** (country/world; the Internet is the largest WAN). Devices: **router** (joins networks), **switch** (joins devices in a LAN), **modem** (digital ↔ analog). An **IP address** identifies a device; **DNS** turns names into IPs.

POP3 110 / IMAP 143 (receive mail)

cards.title: Threats
cards.body: **Phishing**: fake emails/sites to steal credentials. **Vishing**: by phone; **smishing**: by SMS. **Ransomware** encrypts files for ransom. **Trojan** hides inside useful-looking software. **Worm** spreads by itself; a **virus** needs a host file.

cards.title: Banking security terms
cards.body: **OTP/2FA** adds a second factor. **Firewall** filters network traffic. **Encryption** scrambles data. CERT-In is India's national cyber incident agency; report cyber fraud on helpline **1930** or cybercrime.gov.in.

cards.explain: HTTPS (HTTP over TLS) uses port 443; plain HTTP uses 80.

cards.q: A fake SMS asking you to click a link and enter your card PIN is an example of:
cards.explain: Smishing is phishing carried out through SMS.

cards.q: How many layers does the OSI model have?
cards.explain: The OSI reference model has 7 layers: Physical to Application.

notes.p: A **network** connects devices to share data. By area: **PAN** (personal, e.g. Bluetooth), **LAN** (a building), **MAN** (a city), **WAN** (country or world; the Internet is the largest WAN).
points: **Bus:** single backbone cable; a break stops the network.
**Star:** all devices connect to a central hub/switch; most common in offices.
**Ring:** each device connects to two others in a loop.
**Mesh:** many direct connections; highly reliable but costly.
**Transmission modes:** simplex (one way, e.g. TV broadcast), half-duplex (both ways, one at a time, e.g. walkie-talkie), full-duplex (both ways at once, e.g. phone call).

notes.p: The **OSI model** has **7 layers**: **Physical, Data Link, Network, Transport, Session, Presentation, Application**. Memory aid (bottom up): '**P**lease **D**o **N**ot **T**hrow **S**ausage **P**izza **A**way'. The practical **TCP/IP** model has **4 layers**.
points: **Hub** → layer 1 (Physical); **switch** → layer 2 (Data Link, uses MAC addresses); **router** → layer 3 (Network, uses IP addresses).
**MAC address** = 48-bit hardware address of a network card.
**DNS** converts domain names into IP addresses.
**Modem** converts digital signals to analog and back.

notes.p: Each service uses a protocol and a default port number.
points: HTTP 80; **HTTPS 443** (encrypted with TLS).
FTP 20/21 (file transfer); SSH 22; Telnet 23.
SMTP 25 (sending mail); POP3 110 and IMAP 143 (receiving mail).
DNS 53.
A URL like https://www.example.com/page has a protocol (https), domain (example.com) and path (/page).

notes.p: Banking exams focus on threats customers and staff face.
points: **Phishing:** fake emails/websites that steal credentials; **vishing** by voice call; **smishing** by SMS.

**Malware:** **virus** (needs a host file), **worm** (spreads by itself), **Trojan** (hides inside useful-looking software), **ransomware** (encrypts data for ransom), **spyware/keylogger** (records activity).
**DDoS:** floods a server with traffic to make it unavailable.
**SIM swap fraud:** criminal gets a duplicate SIM to receive your OTPs.
**QR code fraud:** you **never need to scan a QR code or enter a UPI PIN to receive money**; a PIN is needed only to pay.
**Remote-access app fraud:** fraudsters ask you to install screen-sharing apps.

notes.p:
A customer gets an SMS: "Your KYC has expired. Click this link and enter your card number and OTP or your account will be blocked."
Step 1: Channel is SMS → this is **smishing** (a form of phishing).
Step 2: Red flags: urgency, a link, request for OTP. Banks never ask for OTP, PIN or CVV.
Step 3: Correct action: do not click; report to the bank and to the national cyber-crime helpline **1930** or cybercrime.gov.in.

Defences: **firewalls** filter traffic, **antivirus** detects malware, **encryption** scrambles data, **two-factor authentication** adds a second check, and **digital signatures** prove authenticity. **CERT-In** is India's national agency for cyber incidents.
Often confused.
points: Virus needs a host; worm does not.
Router = layer 3; switch = layer 2; hub = layer 1.
HTTPS 443, HTTP 80.
SMTP sends mail; POP3/IMAP receive.
Receiving money by UPI never needs a PIN.

points: LAN < MAN < WAN; Internet = largest WAN.
OSI 7 layers; TCP/IP 4 layers.
IPv4 32 bits; IPv6 128 bits; MAC 48 bits.
Phishing (email), vishing (call), smishing (SMS).

notes.p: Computer aptitude is combined with reasoning in several Mains papers (for example the "Reasoning & Computer Aptitude" section in IBPS PO and SBI Clerk Mains) and appears in RRB and SO papers; the exact section split varies by year, so check the current notification. Questions are factual, with frequent repetition of themes: devices, memory, OS, networking, MS Office and security.

**Input:** keyboard, mouse, trackball, joystick, light pen, touch screen, scanner, microphone, webcam, **MICR** (cheques), **OMR** (answer sheets), **OCR** (printed text), barcode/QR scanners, biometric devices.
**Output:** monitor (LCD/LED), printers — **impact** (dot-matrix, line) and **non-impact** (inkjet, laser) — plotters, speakers, projectors.
**Both:** touch screen, modem, network card.

**Worked recall example:** A bank clears cheques in bulk. Device needed? **MICR reader**. A recruiter scans multiple-choice sheets? **OMR**.

**Storage devices:** hard disk (magnetic), **SSD** (flash, faster, no moving parts), pen drive, memory card, optical discs (CD ~700 MB, DVD ~4.7 GB single layer, Blu-ray 25 GB single layer). **Units:** 1 byte = 8 bits; 1 KB = 1,024 bytes; then MB, GB, TB, PB in steps of 1,024.

The CPU fetches, decodes and executes instructions. The **ALU** performs arithmetic and logic; the **control unit** directs operations; **registers** hold data being processed; **cache** keeps frequently used data close to the CPU. Speed is measured in clock cycles (GHz). Multi-core processors run several instruction streams at once.
points: Hierarchy (fastest to slowest): registers → cache → RAM → SSD/HDD.
Microprocessor: a CPU on a single chip.

notes.p:
An OS is system software that manages hardware and offers services to applications.

Functions: **process management** (scheduling programs), **memory management** (allocating RAM, virtual memory), **file management** (folders, permissions), **device management** (drivers) and **security** (user accounts).

Types: **batch**, **time-sharing**, **real-time** (strict deadlines — e.g. ATMs’ embedded controllers, avionics), **distributed**, **mobile** (Android is Linux-based). **Multitasking** runs several tasks on one CPU by switching; **multiprocessing** uses more than one CPU.

**Worked example:** If a 4 GB RAM PC opens programs needing 6 GB, the OS uses **virtual memory** — part of the disk acts as extra RAM, slowing the system (more paging).

**Software types:** **system software** (OS, device drivers, utilities like antivirus and disk cleanup) runs the computer; **application software** (word processors, browsers, banking apps) serves users. **Open-source** software (Linux) allows its code to be studied and changed; **proprietary** software (Windows) does not. **Freeware** is free to use; **shareware** is free to try.
Mix-ups to avoid.

notes.p: Questions on Word, Excel and PowerPoint — especially shortcuts, file extensions and basic Excel formulas — are among the most frequent in bank computer awareness. They are also practical: officers use these tools daily for reports and MIS.

Key features of **MS Word**: formatting (fonts, paragraphs, styles), page layout (margins, orientation), **headers and footers**, **tables**, **mail merge** (personalised letters from a data list), **track changes** and comments, and a generated **table of contents** from heading styles.

Shortcuts often asked: Ctrl+E (centre), Ctrl+J (justify), Ctrl+Enter (page break), F7 (spelling), Shift+F3 (change case), Ctrl+K (insert hyperlink), Ctrl+N (new document).

**Worked recall example:** A branch must send 500 personalised loan-renewal letters. Which Word feature helps? **Mail Merge** — it combines one letter template with a data source (an Excel sheet of names and addresses) to produce individual letters.

In **Excel**, a workbook contains worksheets made of cells; each cell is addressed by column and row. Formulas begin with **=**.

**Worked example 1:** A2:A5 contain 10, 20, 30, 40. =SUM(A2:A5) → **100**; =AVERAGE(A2:A5) → **25**; =COUNT(A2:A5) → **4**; =MAX(A2:A5) → **40**.

**Worked example 2:** B2 holds marks 45. =IF(B2>=40,"Pass","Fail") → **Pass**.

**Worked example 3:** C1 contains =A1*$B$1. Copied to C2, it becomes **=A2*$B$1** — the relative part shifts, the absolute part stays.

**VLOOKUP**(value, table, column number, FALSE) finds a value in the first column of a table and returns a value from another column — useful for customer or branch data.

Other useful functions: **COUNTIF**(range, condition) counts cells meeting a condition; **SUMIF** adds them; **ROUND**(number, digits) rounds; **CONCAT**/& joins text. Error codes: **#DIV/0!** (division by zero), **#N/A** (lookup not found), **#VALUE!** (wrong data type), **#REF!** (invalid reference), **####** (column too narrow).

**PowerPoint** builds slide decks. The **Slide Master** sets fonts, colours and layout for all slides. **Transitions** animate the change between slides; **animations** move objects within a slide. Views: Normal, Slide Sorter, Notes Page, Reading View, Slide Show. F5 starts from the beginning; Shift+F5 from the current slide.

Useful extras: **Ctrl+D** duplicates a slide; **Rehearse Timings** records how long each slide is shown; **Hyperlinks** and **Action buttons** allow non-linear navigation; presentations can be saved as PDF or video.

**Access** is a database (tables, queries, forms, reports). **Outlook** manages email, calendar and contacts. **OneNote** is for notes. Cloud versions (Microsoft 365) allow real-time co-authoring. Equivalent free tools exist, such as LibreOffice and Google Docs, Sheets and Slides.

cards.title: What a DBMS does
cards.body: A **database** is an organised collection of data; a **DBMS** (Oracle, MySQL, SQL Server, MS Access) stores, retrieves, secures and backs it up, and lets many users work at once without corrupting data.

cards.body: Transactions must be **Atomic** (all or nothing), **Consistent**, **Isolated** and **Durable**. A fund transfer that debits one account must also credit the other, or neither happens.

notes.h: Why DBMS appears in bank exams
notes.p:
Banks run on databases: every account, transaction and customer profile sits in a DBMS behind the Core Banking Solution. Computer awareness questions test basic vocabulary — keys, SQL commands, normalisation and ACID — and IBPS SO IT officer papers go deeper.

Before DBMS, data lived in separate **file systems**, causing duplication and inconsistency (the same customer address stored differently in two files). A DBMS centralises data, enforces rules, controls access with user rights, and supports backup and recovery. Database models include **hierarchical**, **network**, **relational** (most common) and **object-oriented**; newer **NoSQL** systems store documents or key–value pairs for very large or flexible datasets.

In a **relational database**, data is held in **tables**. Each row is a **record (tuple)**; each column is a **field (attribute)**. The number of rows is the **cardinality**; the number of columns is the **degree**.

**Keys:** a **primary key** uniquely identifies rows and cannot be NULL; a **candidate key** could serve as primary key; a **foreign key** links to another table’s primary key; a **composite key** uses more than one column.

**Worked example 1:** Table CUSTOMER(CustID, Name, PAN) and ACCOUNT(AccNo, CustID, Balance). Primary keys: CustID and AccNo. In ACCOUNT, **CustID is a foreign key** linking each account to its owner. PAN is a candidate key in CUSTOMER because it is unique per person.

**Normalisation** organises tables to cut redundancy and update anomalies: **1NF** (atomic values), **2NF** (no partial dependency on part of a composite key), **3NF** (no transitive dependency). **Integrity constraints** — NOT NULL, UNIQUE, CHECK, primary and foreign keys — keep data valid. **ACID** properties keep transactions reliable.
points: Data warehouse: large store for analysis; data mining finds patterns in it.
DBA: database administrator.
